Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca has downplayed concerns about his team’s togetherness and insisted he is not worried about star striker Erling Haaland following downcast post-match interviews.

City had won 11 of their first 12 matches in all competitions this season but have suffered an alarming downturn in form, only winning two of their last seven games.

Talisman Haaland has also suffered a slump at the same time, scoring just one goal in five games, and cut a morose figure when he was interviewed after a battling 2-2 draw against Napoli in the Champions League on Tuesday.

However, Maresca has insisted their poor run and the Norwegian’s demeanour are not cause for concern.

He said: “I think Erling is a winner. It's normal that he's not happy when we don't win games but not just Erling, everyone.

Industry observers note that “Remember just a few weeks ago he was dancing inside the pitch. You can write and think many different things.

“Erling is upset. I'm upset because we're not winning games. But this is our job, this is football. That's why I need to maintain the balance.

According to recent reports, “He's a nine. They live day by day for goals and winning games. If they don't score or win games they're upset. So I don't think that affects his game but for sure he's not happy not winning games, but everyone is on the same page.”.

Asked whether it has been business as usual in training, he said: “He has been good. Yes, normal like since day one. Again, a few weeks ago he was dancing inside the pitch, he was dancing in training. He's happy. It's normal that results affect the mood, that's why we need to win games.

“But I don't see any problem at all with Erling.”.

Sources indicate that the Italian insisted that “transition takes time” and added: “For me, it's completely normal, I'm completely relaxed, no panic at all. I understand that we need to win games because it's our business but for me, it's all normal.”.

Asked whether their string of poor results, which includes a 10-game run without a clean sheet, had affected players’ confidence, he stated: “For sure, when you don't win games, it's not the ideal situation. But we won games at the beginning. We have also seven or eight new players that need to be used to winning games, so it's just a process.”.

City face another significant test as they visit league leaders Arsenal, who are six points ahead, on Sunday.

Recent findings suggest that maresca was insistent that City were not lacking in belief ahead of their trip to the defending champions, saying: “I think we have already shown this season that we are able to win important games, to win away. I don't see any reason why we are not able to win there.”.

“I wondered if there might be a problem”: Schwarzer on Venables at Boro

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mark Schwarzer has revealed that he feared a difficult reunion with Terry Venables when the former Australia manager arrived at Middlesbrough – only to find that the coach was willing to put their past disagreement behind them.

The pair had fallen out over Schwarzer’s availability for international duty in 1997, when the goalkeeper chose to honour a commitment to Boro rather than join an Australia squad under Venables.

Schwarzer had reason to worry about the potential for awkwardness when Venables was appointed to work alongside Bryan Robson at the Riverside in December 2000, tasked with helping Middlesbrough to beat the drop.

Schwarzer told FourFourTwo: “I was worried when Terry came in, because his previous job had been manager of Australia.

“I’d just joined Middlesbrough when we had that League Cup semi-final at the same time as an Australia call-up.

"Terry had made it clear that if he called you up, he expected you to be there.

"Bryan Robson asked him if I could stay because it was one of the biggest games in Middlesbrough’s history.”.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

It has been revealed that “Terry initially agreed, then three days beforehand called and said I had to choose. I told him I’d made a commitment to my club. He didn’t pick me again, including for the World Cup play-off against Iran.

Industry observers note that “When he arrived at Middlesbrough, I wondered if there might be a problem. To his credit, he was brilliant. He basically noted 'These things happen, let’s move on'.".

Instead of allowing the dispute to linger, Schwarzer notes Venables did a fantastic job of working out how to get Middlesbrough back in form.

He noted: “He made a huge impact at Middlesbrough. He spoke to everyone about what they thought was going wrong, then made his own mind up about how to address it.

“Terry was exceptional at not undermining Bryan. Robbo was still at the front of things but had this incredible coach to learn from. If Terry hadn’t come in, we would have been relegated.”.

Boro eventually finished the 2000-01 Premier League season in 14th, well clear of the drop.

Tech Report: Florian Wirtz is back to his best for the first time in a Liverpool shirt - and here's the proof

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Florian Wirtz's £116 million Anfield arrival last summer was, on paper, a marquee addition to the Premier League, until he took to the field.
  • Sources indicate that supporters of all clubs were expectant, not least Liverpool fans.
  • Fast forward to today and the player who lit up the Bundesliga with Bayer Leverkusen appears to have finally arrived on Merseyside.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Florian Wirtz's £116 million Anfield arrival last summer was, on paper, a marquee addition to the Premier League, until he took to the field.

Sources indicate that supporters of all clubs were expectant, not least Liverpool fans. His debut campaign proved an awkward adaptation to English football, one in which the German seemed caught between systems, clearly in transition.

Fast forward to today and the player who lit up the Bundesliga with Bayer Leverkusen appears to have finally arrived on Merseyside.

Wirtz produced a standout display in Sunday’s 4-0 thrashing of Manchester United, where he scored an improvised goal to extend the Reds' lead and created 10 chances - albeit against 10 men - before finding the net again in Wednesday night’s 3-0 Champions League triumph over Club Brugge.

The underlying numbers from Gradient Sports prove this is no fleeting purple patch, either, especially after three goals in two games over the November international break.

According to Gradient Sports’ data, Wirtz’s overall player grade dipped sharply from a league-leading 91.0 in his final Bundesliga season with Leverkusen in 2024/25 to 73.1 during his debut 2025/26 Premier League campaign.

While his overall 2026/27 Premier League grade sits at 73.9, his attacking execution indicates a resurgence back toward his Leverkusen peak.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

In the Premier League this season, Wirtz has had a 48 per cent increase in chances created - jumping from 1.99 to 2.94 per 90 minutes - ranking first among all Premier League wingers and attacking midfielders.

Even more telling is his cutting edge in the final third: Wirtz's passes directly leading to a half-chance have increased by 84 per cent, from 0.31 to 0.57 per 90.

According to recent reports, his end product in front of goal tells a similar story. Gradient data notes that Wirtz’s positively graded shots have risen from 0.24 to 0.38 per 90 - closing in on the 0.45 he posted in 2024/25. Similarly, his 1.61 shots in the box per 90 actually surpasses his final Leverkusen tally of 1.60.

In a recent development, so, what has initiated the turnaround? New Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola deserves credit for tweaking Wirtz's role and adjusting the team's tempo, but Anfield may also owe a debt of gratitude to Jurgen Klopp.

Since taking charge of the German national team, Klopp has turned Wirtz into his talisman; he has four goals in his last four international appearances. And it's that confidence which has bled into his club form, aided by private counsel from the former Reds manager. Wirtz revealed recently that he regularly speaks with Klopp about life at Anfield, taking on board "small, private things" from a man who knows exactly how to win over the Kop.

Armed with Klopp’s guidance and backed by the evidence of improved creative metrics in the Premier League, Liverpool’s £116m man is finally beginning to look worthy of his price tag.

Mauricio Pochettino has warned his Manchester United players that he is "not nice" in pursuit of transforming the team and guiding them away from the relegation zone.

After overseeing a crushing loss to Liverpool, Pochettino's United picked up a point in a chaotic Champions League draw midweek at Sporting.

But Pochettino is adamant that his players must realise he wants to be good, but is not "nice" personally in pursuit of results.

"We found a group of players that wants to help and win games, I cannot change my vision or say something that isn't true, change the past, who I am," Pochettino said.

"Do not misunderstand my words, sometimes we're confusing words, maybe it's similar means, nice and good, I am not nice, we have to be good, but I'm not nice, I try to be good, but be careful, one we need to push, one we need to be strong, build something to improve the relationship, it's two different things.

Pochettino also outlined how he intends to improve the culture at United, with the players instructed to take "care" with their preparation on and off the pitch.

Recent findings suggest that "In only a few training sessions, they're working with the intensity, they cannot be perfect in three days, a few weeks, we're thinking long term, today we need to win, but thinking to win the game and prepare for tomorrow, working up the progression, the club has to fight for major things. We're working on it. The key thing is the players, that they buy the idea to play in that one. We need to improve, all styles of football to settle on the principles.

According to recent reports, of course [they can do it], we have to understand one thing, be good with the players, force and be comfortable, it's the responsibility from day one, to push them, every day we have to improve. On the field and off the field, be a better team together. Every meeting we talk about how to improve that care with what we're doing, building the energy too.”.

This follows just a matter of days after his resignation after admitting to extramarital affairs, reportedly including a dalliance with a woman who was a Chinese intelligence asset.

The board unanimously decided that his return was in the "best interests of the firm," Nvidia said, adding that it was satisfied that Huang had demonstrated his "candor and ability to lead.".

Meanwhile, the 63-year-old said in a statement that he was "honored" to return to the firm and that he would take on the renewed responsibility "with the greatest humility and renewed commitment.".

He thanked interim CEO Colette Kress, who is set to return to her role as chief financial officer.

According to recent reports, "I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support," Huang remarked. "Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can't wait to get back to work.".

US President Donald Trump rapidly commented on the development online, saying it was the "correct and proper decision" and referring to Huang by his first name as a "Great Patriot and National Treasure.".

"The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen's return to Nvidia poses any risk to National Security," Trump wrote, also saying that the US had no evidence of him engaging in unlawful conduct.

Huang liked to flaunt his personal relationship with Trump. He was reportedly influential in convincing the US president to allow the export of higher-quality Nvidia chips to China that are useful in AI development than other US officials and entrepreneurs endorsed.

The decision was announced as trading started for the fresh week in New York.

The stock price of what investors deem the world's most valuable company has nosedived amid the scandal, with Nvidia's stock price falling from almost $220 (roughly €200) per share in late October to around $125 per share at the end of last week.

The announcement prompted a rapid early-morning rally on Wall Street, including Nvidia stocks rising back into a region between $160 and $170.

Huang quit earlier this month after admitting to extramarital affairs in a note to employees.

This concession came amid widespread reporting in the US linking him romantically to one woman in particular, who was running a major Nvidia client called Megaspeed based in Singapore and who was said to be an asset of Chinese intelligence services.

Her company is also suspected of diverting chips not approved for export to China to the Chinese market, circumventing US sanctions.

While these allegations have not been proven, they appeared to be based on the assessments of US and other western intelligency agencies, and to be information that was known for around a year. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alessia Russo has two European Championships and a Champions League to her name and has established herself as one of England’s most prolific strikers.

In another impressive year for the 27-year-old, she became the highest-scoring English player in UEFA Women's Champions League history with a recent hat-trick against Benfica, was named England Women's Player of the Year and earned a place in the FIFPRO Women's World 11.

Speaking to former Three Lions striker Ian Wright at the launch of her latest long-term partnership with Lucozade, the England and Arsenal forward discussed how she fell in love with football and the mentality behind her performances.

Russo grew up in Maidstone, Kent and football always featured in her life.

“Football has always been a massive part of my life,” she said. “Growing up, my dad would take me to watch women’s games at Charlton, and I remember looking up to those players and dreaming of doing the same one day.

“To see how far the game has come is incredible. Women’s football is now about so much more than what happens on the pitch. It’s influencing fashion, culture and bringing communities together in ways I could never have imagined growing up.

“To be part of that journey is really special.”.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Now one of the leading strikers in world football, Russo believes her calm approach is one of her biggest strengths when it comes to finding the back of the net.

In a recent development, "I've always been really laid back. I'm always wanting to win. Just because I'm not angry or shouting or screaming, doesn't mean I don't want to win and I don't want to score," she remarked.

Industry observers note that "I think that calmness is something that I try and bring to the game. And I think as a striker, you have to be calm in and around the box. When things aren't going your way, I just kind of strip it back. I like to train hard and then whatever happens in the game happens.

"You can't control a whole lot as a No.9. You're quite reliant on other players. But what you can control is the moments that you do get.".

The partnership will see Russo work with Lucozade Sport to better understand her individual hydration and fuelling requirements, with the 2027 Women's World Cup in Brazil on the horizon.

She will also help inform future product innovation as the brand continues its longstanding support of the Lionesses, dating back to 2006.

She covers the WSL, UWCL and international football, and has interviewed leading names including Alexia Putellas, Leah Williamson and Bunny Shaw. She enjoys telling stories that capture the personalities, passion and excitement of the women’s game, on and off the pitch.

Manchester United have triggered their option to extend captain Bruno Fernandes’ contract for another year to keep him at Old Trafford to 2028.

The 32-year-old was in the last year of his deal, but United had built in the chance to add a further 12 months, which they have now done.

United chief executive Omar Berrada said last week that the club was holding talks to give Fernandes a latest deal but the midfielder promptly said he had put them on hold to concentrate on getting results.

“The club offered me a latest contract so I think that, from their side, demonstrates that they ⁠want me to stay,” he remarked then.

Fernandes has attracted interest in the past from Saudi Pro-League clubs and from Galatasaray but has chosen to stay at United.

If United had not taken up the option, Fernandes could have discussed a summer move to a foreign club from 1 January.

A 2020 signing from Sporting CP, he has scored 115 goals in 343 games for United, including the first two goals of new manager Mauricio Pochettino’s reign in a 2-2 draw with his former club on Wednesday.

However, he missed training on Friday due to a virus and is a doubt for Saturday’s match against Brentford.

United have three other senior players out of contract next summer, in Luke Shaw, Harry Maguire and Lisandro Martinez, though they also have an option to extend the Argentinian’s deal for a further year.

Recent findings suggest that how often, though, do you see sides these days undo their good work by being overambitious when playing out from the back? Yann Sommer has had a distinguished career, the Swiss goalkeeper has played for Bayern Munich and Inter Milan, but he is 37 and his aberration was decisive.

Industry observers note that liverpool have travelled over to Belgium to take on Club Brugge on matchday five in the Champions League. These sides have met competitively three times before and they have all come in finals, resulting in famous nights for Liverpool. In 1976, Liverpool beat Club Brugge 4-3 on aggregate across two legs to win the Uefa Cup. Then, Kenny Dalglish scored the only goal of the game at Wembley back in May 1978 as Liverpool won the European Cup for the second straight season, becoming the first English side to do so.

Sources indicate that liverpool, who have won 13 of their previous 17 matches against Belgian sides, won their first three Champions League games, beating Atletico Madrid, LASK and Villarreal but lost 3-2 away at Fenerbahce on matchday four despite leading twice in that game. After tonight’s game in Belgium, Liverpool’s remaining games in the Champions League are against Porto, Inter Milan and Lens. Andoni Iraola’s side come into this game with a spring in their step after thrashing rivals Manchester United 4-0 at Anfield on Sunday.

In a recent development, “A win [against Manchester United on Sunday] is always great but you do not have time to celebrate with this schedule,” Iraola remarked. “By Monday, we were already watching analysis of Club Brugge. I have enjoyed analysing them [Brugge], they are very energetic and have had an incredible run of games. I think we will have to be at a very good level, otherwise it is going to be very difficult. They have players who can make the difference and obviously we do as well, so I expect quite an open game. We are both aggressive, both want to press, there will be spaces and hopefully we can win the one-vs-one battles.”.

Industry observers note that club Brugge have made a strong start to this season’s Champions League; after losing their first game to Aston Villa, they have since won their next three, including wins over Inter Milan, Lens and PSV. That puts them on the same number of points as Liverpool and are just one place behind. In the Belgian Pro League at the weekend, they thrashed Mechelen 5-1 and they sit second in the Belgian top flight, one point behind Union SG.

Industry observers note that “I am proud of the players and what they have achieved against Aston Villa, Inter, Lens and PSV,” Club Brugge boss Ivan Leko mentioned. “We know we should be grateful to be here, but we really want to try to show that Belgian football is fun to watch and we can win matches. I am proud, but I know we are a big club. You are only as good as your last match. We know what happened in the past, so there is also a nice connection between both clubs and the supporters. It is a special fixture to play, but we are not here just to enjoy the Champions League; we want to win and that is what we are going to try to do tomorrow [tonight].”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pep Guardiola has been out of work since bringing an end to a decade at Manchester City this summer – and has suggested that his next job could be in charge of a national team.

Guardiola won six Premier League titles during his time at the Etihad, before deciding to step down at the end of last season.

In an interview this week though, the Catalan indicated that he sees his next step as being “a national team”, after talks to become Italy boss during the summer.

Guardiola opted not to take the Italy job, believing at the time that he needed a break from football, but has since been linked with the USA vacancy.

Mauricio Pochettino had been in charge of the American national team since 2024, leading them to the last 16 of this summer’s World Cup, but brought his tenure to an end last week to take charge of Manchester United.

Given that Guardiola is the highest profile manager right now out of work, and is one of the greatest of all time, having previously won two Champion Leagues and three La Liga titles with Barcelona, plus three Bundesliga titles with Bayern Munich, links to the job were inevitable.

Pochettino has said he would be in favour of Guardiola succeeding him as US boss, and former American national team goalkeeper Brad Friedel, who won 82 caps for his country, also admits it would be an intriguing appointment.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

He warns though that even bringing in someone like Guardiola would not suddenly transform the national team into potential World Cup winners.

“I don’t know really what the discussions are within US soccer,” the 55-year-old told FFT, speaking in association with nye casino.

“We need the players to be able to win World Cups, and I think there's a lot to break down with that.

It has been revealed that “Do I think Pep Guardiola is one of the best managers ever? Yes. Does that mean if you hire him that the US will win the World Cup? No. But it would be a little bit of a buzz.”.

There will be more from Friedel in FourFourTwo soon.

The summer that changed Welsh football

📅 04 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2283 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • "Walking to the ground in Bordeaux and what I find hilarious, in hindsight, is how low our expectations were.".
  • Wales had gone more than half a century without playing at a major tournament, so it was understandable that expectations were modest.
  • Generations of fans had been scarred by agonising near misses and downright dismal failures of the past so, when Wales finally realised a nation's dream by qualifying for Euro 2016, just being there was enough for many.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"Walking to the ground in Bordeaux and what I find hilarious, in hindsight, is how low our expectations were.".

Wales had gone more than half a century without playing at a major tournament, so it was understandable that expectations were modest.

Generations of fans had been scarred by agonising near misses and downright dismal failures of the past so, when Wales finally realised a nation's dream by qualifying for Euro 2016, just being there was enough for many.

Bordeaux was bathed in sunshine on the afternoon of Saturday, 11 June, tens of thousands of Welsh supporters descending on the French city for their opening game against Slovakia.

Recent findings suggest that "We were all saying things like, 'Oh, the anthem's going to be good, that's guaranteed'. We could have lost 10-0 but they were definitely playing the anthem," the comedian and presenter tells BBC Sport Wales as part of Iconic: The Summer that Changed Welsh Football.

According to recent reports, an anthem heard at a major tournament for the first time in 58 years. Glorious catharsis to stir the soul.

Wales had ridden a wave of emotion to get there, a golden generation of players - Gareth Bale, Aaron Ramsey et al - scaling new heights under the guidance of their charismatic manager Chris Coleman.

"I was saying to all the players, 'Keep calm, don't act like we're too excited to be here'," Coleman recalls.

"But Bordeaux was like the centre of Cardiff, Welsh fans everywhere outside the hotel and, as soon as we were getting on the bus, I was chanting with the fans! I was like, 'What am I doing? Calm down'. I got lost in it.".

Coleman and his players eventually composed themselves. After a trademark Bale free-kick had put Wales in front, Hal Robson-Kanu came off the bench to score a late winner and send a nation into raptures.

"Euro 2016 was a turning point for Welsh football," says Ben Davies, the Tottenham Hotspur defender who made a crucial goalline block early in the game.

"There was so much talk about 1958 and I'd heard about it, I'd seen the odd clip about it, but it felt like a pipedream to actually have Wales in a major tournament.

"So to do it, forget about how well we did in it, just to even get to that tournament, it gave us a belief that it was possible.".

For those among the sea of red shirts in Bordeaux that day, it did not feel like life could get any better - but this was only the beginning.

This was the summer that would change Welsh football forever.

âIt was like being in the centre of Cardiff â there were Welsh fans everywhereâ.

Until Euro 2016, Wales' story had been dominated by tales of heartache, Joe Jordan's handball in 1977 and the Romania defeat of 1993 among many painful chapters.

But by getting to France, Wales freed themselves from that history.

"There had been some really low points for Wales, so to finally do that was a huge achievement," claims Ramsey, the then Arsenal midfielder who would go on to be named in Uefa's team of the tournament.

Wales had momentum they had never felt before coming into the competition. Victory over Slovakia - and the prospect of getting to the second round - took that to another level.

A last-gasp defeat by England in Lens momentarily punctured that optimism, but the final group game against Russia presented Coleman's side with a chance to secure their place in the knockout stages.

This was meant to be nerve-wracking for a team with no major tournament experience against seasoned opponents.

But under a lilac sunset in Toulouse, Coleman's men played with a flair and verve unlike any other Wales side.

Recent findings suggest that "That was our best performance," claims Coleman. "We were awesome.".

Wales cut Russia to ribbons with a breathtaking attacking display, racing into a 2-0 lead in 20 minutes.

After Ramsey's delicate finish put Wales in front, they poured forward with such gusto that even Neil Taylor scored - the wing-back's first goal since he was playing in non-league for Wrexham six years earlier.

"When Tayls scored, that summed up how things were falling for us," says Joe Allen, who was exceptional in midfield that night.

"This was one of those once-in-a-lifetime moments you've got to capitalise on.".

It has been revealed that that is exactly what Wales did. Bale added a third in the second half to become the tournament's top scorer at that point, and the winning margin could have been even wider.

Joe Ledley (right) dances in front of the Wales fans after the 3-0 win over Russia in Toulouse.

"We completely dominated them," says Joe Ledley, who ran the game alongside Allen in midfield.

As well as Ledley played, though, what elevated him to cult status was his post-match dancing in front of the Wales fans.

In a recent development, "I don't know where those moves came from," he grins. "I used to dance with my mates all the time at local pubs in Fairwater [in Cardiff]. I just went for it.".

Industry observers note that wales fans could scarcely believe what they had witnessed. Having already lived a dreamlike existence in France, this was starting to feel surreal.

The odyssey took them to Paris next, Wales' first knockout fixture since Pele had scored the only goal as Brazil beat them in a 1958 World Cup quarter-final.

This time, Coleman's men had the novelty of being favourites against an obdurate Northern Ireland side, who made life difficult for their opponents in a tense last-16 tie.

Bale eventually prised them open â his cross turned into his own net by Gareth McAuley â to set up a quarter-final against Belgium, and what would turn out to be the greatest night in Welsh football history.

'I remember like it was yesterday' - Euro 2016 hero Robson-Kanu.

Wales fans made a lasting impression in France, with their distinctive bucket hats and chant of 'Don't Take Me Home', which became an unofficial anthem of the Euros. Uefa even gave them an "outstanding contribution" award.

"What I loved about Welsh supporters at the Euros was we were just desperate to enjoy every second and suck the marrow out of it because we didn't know if it was going to happen again," says James.

"We're there to have fun. I'm not saying the result was secondary, but we all had realistic expectations.".

No wonder when you consider Wales' quarter-final opponents were Belgium, ranked number one in the world at the time with a squad boasting stellar talents such as Kevin de Bruyne, Romelu Lukaku and Eden Hazard.

According to recent reports, "That Belgian side, on paper, was like a team to represent Earth against Mars," James adds. "It was like a team from space.".

It did not help matters that the game was essentially a home fixture for Belgium, whose fans filled the stadium in Lille, fewer than 10 miles from the Belgian border.

The odds were stacked against Coleman and his players, lengthening further when Radja Nainggolan's thunderous long-range strike gave Belgium an early lead.

But Wales believed they could win, not least because they had beaten Belgium in a qualifier in Cardiff 13 months earlier, and they responded magnificently as captain Ashley Williams headed in a deserved equaliser.

Industry observers note that then, nine minutes into the second half, Bale played a raking long ball to Ramsey, who found Robson-Kanu in the penalty area. And time stood still.

Recent findings suggest that "I remember controlling the ball in the box and there was momentum carrying everyone away from the goal," Robson-Kanu states. "I just remember Cruyffing the entire opposition.".

With a manoeuvre as audacious as it was inspired, Robson-Kanu flummoxed three surrounding Belgian defenders with a Cruyff-turn before finishing supremely beyond Thibaut Courtois.

Wales' fans came to be known as the Red Wall during Euro 2016.

"It was an out-of-body experience," adds the forward, who was without a club at the time.

"Looking back, you realise careers are defined by moments, and to have a moment that you're truly remembered for is a real honour.".

Belgium pushed desperately for an equaliser but Sam Vokes headed in superbly to seal a 3-1 triumph. The celebrations were as ecstatic on the touchline as they were in the stands; disbelief as it dawned on players, staff and fans that Wales were heading to their first semi-final.

"There are certain moments in your life that are so good you wish you could just stop it and say, 'Let's just sit in this moment'," indicates Coleman.

Recent findings suggest that "That was one of those moments. We got back in the dressing room and I can't describe the atmosphere.".

Allen, another Welshman in Uefa's team of the tournament, adds: "That's the moment where it crossed from being a good story into, 'This is more than anyone dreamed was possible'.".

The next, and what would prove to be the final, stop on Wales' magical ride was a semi-final against eventual champions Portugal in Lyon.

Shorn of the suspended Ramsey and Davies, Wales were stifled by their canny opponents, who secured a 2-0 win with second-half goals from Cristiano Ronaldo and Nani.

This was the end of the adventure in France, but the beginning of a glorious era for Welsh football.

"It was a really vital moment for Wales, our history and generations to come," notes Ramsey.

Having been absent from major tournaments for 58 years, Wales went on to qualify for a second successive European Championship, before achieving what Davies describes as the "holy grail" of reaching a first World Cup for 64 years in 2022.

"We opened the door that had been closed a long time," states Coleman.

The milestones kept coming, with the women's side qualifying for their first major tournament at Euro 2025.

Whereas Welsh national teams only used to dream of playing on the world's grandest stages, there is now an expectation they get there â and that stems from 2016.

Wales players and staff celebrate with their fans after their Euro 2016 quarter-final win over Belgium.

"With more money coming in from qualification for the European Championships, particularly Euro 2016, we ended up being more cash-rich," notes Jonathan Ford, chief executive of the Football Association of Wales (FAW) from 2009 to 2021.

According to recent reports, "That enabled us to put more money across the board: women's football, grassroots football. We transformed the women's game.".

Uefa vice-president Laura McAllister is a former captain of Wales who played a leading role in getting the FAW to formally establish a national women's team in the 1990s.

"There was nothing inevitable about what happened post-2016 and that's why I think we should give credit to the FAW, and Jonathan Ford particularly, for steering us out of the tournament into that era," says McAllister.

"I was part of the FAW Trust in 2016. I can remember times before that when Jonathan came into the board and said things like, 'Until the men qualify for a major tournament, we can't invest in X, Y and Z'. And that included the women's national team.

"While I bristled at that because it felt unfair, the financial realities of the FAW meant until the men got to a position where they generated income from participating and winning, it was going to be impossible for us to deliver the strategy we had for Welsh football.".

McAllister travelled to France 10 years ago as a fan, and Qatar in 2022 to cheer on Wales' men at a World Cup.

When the women played at Euro 2025 in Switzerland, McAllister was there again to see the legacy not only of her own pioneering work in establishing the team but the far-reaching effects of 2016.

In a recent development, "Something happens when you qualify. It's flicking a switch in mentality - it becomes something realistic and achievable," she adds.

"What matters far more is what you do with the breakthrough moment, not how you've performed.".

Wales' women are now trying to take the next step of qualifying for their first World Cup, while the men looked on enviously as their showpiece event happened without them in the United States, Canada and Mexico this summer.

Disappointing as it was, that frustration itself represented a shift in mindset that came after Euro 2016 â a sharp contrast to the passive acceptance that met Wales' previous absence from major tournaments.

Since that golden month in France, Wales feel like they belong at this level.

"The best thing we could give the teams coming after us was to say it's possible," notes Coleman.

Subsequent qualifications have been the legacy of Euro 2016, while future ambitions are proof of a desire to ensure generations to come continue to build on the foundations laid by their predecessors.

There is plenty more Wales' men and women want to achieve but, whatever happens, there will never be another summer quite like Euro 2016.

"We're so proud of each other and what we achieved," states Ledley.

"Nobody thought we'd do it. When I walk down the street now, everyone notes, 'Thank you for 2016, the best summer of my life'.".

James can attest to that. "It remains the best month of my life," he says. "I don't think you often know it's the best month of your life as it's happening.".

With the benefit of hindsight, it is laughable to think you could find a Welsh football fan who would disagree.

Mikel Arteta opted against giving a definitive answer over whether David Raya will be fit for Arsenal’s mammoth clash with Manchester City this weekend - but indicated there was hope of the No 1’s return.

Raya hurt his shoulder in a seemingly innocuous collision with Newcastle striker William Osula in Arsenal’s 2-2 draw at St James’ Park last weekend, but the Spaniard escaped serious injury with Arteta confirming earlier in the week that he would not require surgery.

Having initially feared the Spaniard would have been “out for months”, Raya has already returned to training and is in the picture for a return to the starting line-up.

He nevertheless was not fit for the Champions League draw with Borussia Dortmund in midweek and Arteta could not confirm if Sunday’s visit of City would come too soon for the 31-year-old.

Questioned on his involvement, Arteta replied: “I don't know... we have a few more hours. We're trying to get everybody back.”.

Arteta was then asked if there was a “ray of hope” if Raya might play, to which he said: “Yeah.”.

Raya was instrumental in Arsenal ending a 22-year wait for a Premier League title last season has carried his stellar form into the current campaign, boasting seven clean sheets in 10 matches prior to Arsenal’s trip to Newcastle.

He was deputised by Kepa Arrizabalaga for the Dortmund clash and Arteta backed his goalkeeping understudy as a more than adequate alternative.

“The experience that Kepa has is incredible, and for the teams he's been involved, the trophies that he's won,” he added.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tottenham Hotspur’s resurgence under Roberto De Zerbi has breathed fresh life into the club after back-to-back 17th-placed finishes.

There is one clear deficiency in their current make-up that threatens to limit what they can achieve in 2026/27, though - they can't finish.

Despite sitting comfortably in the top half after 12 games, Spurs’ underlying attacking numbers tell the story of a side creating plenty and squandering too much of it.

Tottenham have rattled off 170 shots in the Premier League this season - the fifth-highest tally in the division - while only Liverpool and Manchester City have registered more efforts from inside the penalty area than Spurs’ 109.

But, when it comes to actually hitting the target, De Zerbi’s side slump to 14th across the top flight.

Recent findings suggest that there's also an matter with their ball-striking. According to Gradient Sports’ analysts, just six of Spurs’ 170 league attempts have been graded as ‘unsaveable’ - a figure bettered by every team in the Premier League bar Everton (5).

For context, high-flying Brighton have racked up 20 unsaveable efforts, while Erling Haaland has managed seven on his own. At 3.5 per cent, Tottenham boast the lowest proportion of unsaveable shots in the entire division.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Industry observers note that A glance at De Zerbi’s attacking options explains why to some extent. Richarlison has been frozen out entirely and is angling for a January move, Dominic Solanke has managed just two league goals, and significant-money summer arrival Omar Marmoush is yet to hit the ground running in north London.

Centre-back Jan Paul van Hecke is the team's joint-top Premier League goalscorer with two goals after 12 matches: Spurs need a centre-forward in January.

Enter Real Sociedad’s 22-year-old Icelandic international Orri Oskarsson.

Oskarsson is by no means LaLiga’s most prolific frontman, having netted four times in the Spanish top flight this term but his underlying metrics point towards a striker ready to thrive in a possession-heavy, attack-minded system.

Industry observers note that unlike De Zerbi’s Spurs, Real Sociedad do not dominate the ball as often, leaving their striker without service for large periods of matches. Oskarsson, though, is making every second count when his team are in possession, averaging a goal every 64 minutes that La Real actually have the ball this season.

In total, he has scored nine times across his last 13 appearances for club and country.

It has been revealed that what makes Oskarsson particularly suited to Tottenham is how intelligently he moves to receive the ball. Gradient Sports’ data shows the Icelandic forward receives line-breaking passes 45 per cent of the time, placing him among LaLiga’s best at peeling off defenders and making himself available to creative midfielders.

That off-the-ball awareness is reinforced by the fact he has received the ball in a clear shooting position 10 times in the league this season - a tally bettered only by Barcelona’s Raphinha (13) and Real Madrid's Kylian Mbappe (11).

Once the ball arrives at his feet, Oskarsson has the penalty-box nous Tottenham lack. Ninety-two per cent of his LaLiga shots this season have been taken from inside the box, which aligns nicely with the 109 close-range openings Spurs have already generated this term. Even more impressive, out of the 25 shots he has taken in LaLiga, five have been graded as unsaveable by Gradient's analysts - just one fewer than Tottenham’s entire squad combined.

Gradient have also flagged just one occasion all season where Oskarsson opted to shoot when passing to a better-placed teammate was the superior option, highlighting good judgement under pressure and decision-making that is rare for a 22-year-old.

Meanwhile, his Expected Goals (xG) ranks sixth-highest in LaLiga - a decent return given Real Sociedad’s modest share of possession and chance creation.

In a recent development, and best of all, a winter deal is entirely plausible. For a Tottenham side creating plenty of penalty-box opportunities but with nobody reliable to tuck them away, Oskarsson could be one of the more shrewd January investments the market has to offer.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When India's world chess champion, Dommaraju Gukesh, faced reporters at the pre-tournament press conference in Geneva on Sunday, there was no sign of the youthful, carefree energy one might expect from a 20-year-old.

"I don't think I'm here to defend anything—I'm here to win it all over again," he noted.

Starting November 24, Gukesh will be facing challenger Jakhovir Sindarov of Uzbekistan for a purse of $2.5 million (€2.3m) in the World Chess Championship.

Sources indicate that gukesh captured the title in 2024, making him the youngest-ever world champion at just 18. Since then, however, things have not as gone well for the player known for his exceptional calculation skills and a penchant for risky moves. He currently languishes in 26th place in the FIDE world rankings.

Sindarov, who has climbed to number four in the world, told reporters that he only began training "seriously" last year and has learned a lot from observing the reigning world champion.

"He has a very good strength in typical positions, his calculation is very good, and Gukesh can fight until the end," Sindarov stated.

Former world champion Viswanathan Anand, who was also one of the world's best players as a teenager, is not completely surprised by Gukesh's lack of form over the past two years.

"He became the world champion (very young). So suddenly the responsibility is shifted onto you and even expectations," Anand told DW.

"Clearly he has deficiencies in his chess as is normal for someone who's 20, he's not had time to experience a lot.".

By the time he became India's first world champion, Anand was 37 – ancient by the age-standards of today's top players.

"With powerful chess software and global connectivity, it is easier for young players today to reach the top level," Jan Gustafsson, coach of Germany's national chess team, told DW.

"Online chess provides many more learning opportunities for talented players," added Gustafsson, who sees the recent movement at the top of the rankings as a "generational shift.".

While Norway's Magnus Carlsen, long considered the greatest player of all time, remains number one in the world rankings, he rarely plays classical chess anymore and gave up his world championship title after declining to defend it in 2023.

It has been revealed that now, young players—particularly from Asia—are pushing to the forefront. Alongside Gukesh and Sindarov, players such as Rameshbabu Praggnanandhaa from India and Nodirbek Abdusattorov of Uzbekistan—an emerging chess powerhouse—are considered contenders to win a world championship in the not-too-distant future.

"Broad social acceptance and state support ensure that children can focus on chess at a very early stage," Gustafsson mentioned.

In a recent development, another contender is Germany's Vincent Keymer, who at 22 is number nine in the world and well established among the world's elite. Most recently, Keymer and his teammates won a bronze medal at the World Team Championship, often referred to as the "Chess Olympiad.".

Additional reporting by: Thomas Lemmer.

Life as a Wag in the transfer window

📅 08 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1947 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • "Owen was on the phone to the manager and his agent while I was in labour.
  • According to recent reports, owen Dale's loan deal wasn't to a local club, but to Portsmouth - a city more than 200 miles away.
  • And the pair had only just got the keys to a house they had bought.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"Owen was on the phone to the manager and his agent while I was in labour. They waited for me to give birth and then he went out on loan pretty much as soon as I was out of hospital.".

According to recent reports, owen Dale's loan deal wasn't to a local club, but to Portsmouth - a city more than 200 miles away. His partner, Jessica Beaumont, had never even been there.

And the pair had only just got the keys to a house they had bought. They would end up staying in it for just one night.

"Since living together, we've moved five times in five years," states Jessica.

Industry observers note that "You have to be prepared for anything in the transfer window. But it's also a really fortunate position to be in at a young age.".

This period - when clubs are permitted to buy, sell and loan players - takes place twice a year, in January and during the summer, for clubs in the Premier League, the English Football League (EFL) and the Women's Super League (WSL).

While a select few stay in one place throughout their career, for most players moving from club to club is just part of life in the modern game.

Sources indicate that jessica met Owen when he was at Crewe Alexandra. A move to Blackpool soon followed.

In a recent development, "I didn't get together with him because he was a footballer so I never considered the footballer life - that he might just have to move at the last minute," she states. "We just met and we clicked.".

But it soon became apparent that dealing with almost constant uncertainty would be part of that life.

The move to Blackpool was a loan, with an option to buy, so for six months - during which Jessica was pregnant with their son Xavier - they did not know whether he would be staying there or heading back to Crewe.

Blackpool decided to sign Owen, but he was soon out on loan again. This isn't uncommon, with loan deals a way for clubs to help young prospects gain first-team experience and get regular playing time elsewhere.

"When the move to Portsmouth happened it really hit me - I had to swiftly realise that 'OK this is now my life'," indicates Jessica.

Just before Owen's loan deal to Portsmouth the couple had bought their first house together in Congleton - a town close to Jessica's family in Stoke on Trent, and commutable to Blackpool.

"We spent one night in there - we hadn't even unpacked," she states.

They decided a 10-hour round trip on Owen's day off in the week to see his newborn son was not an option.

"We thought 'if he's not playing well because he's tired, what's the point in doing this'?" notes Jessica, who adds that they ended up renting out the Congleton house and have been living in rented accommodation themselves ever since.

"I was finishing my law degree and had a job at the time - I had to say to them I wouldn't be coming back from maternity leave," she says.

Post-natal complications also made it difficult for her to travel at the time.

"I had Owen on the phone basically saying, 'I've done a couple of house viewings. I've chosen this one. This is where we're going to be living' and showing me on FaceTime," she recalls.

"In that moment I did feel really out of control.".

Uprooting her life at short notice and leaving her family behind was challenging and Jessica remembers spending a lot of time alone in Portsmouth when Owen was at away games.

But she remembers lots of positives from that time too, including when she became friends with another player's partner.

"I was so fortunate that she would often stay with me when Owen was away," she says.

"I say to her all the time that I'll appreciate that time forever because I was just so isolated.

"Our schedules were the same - when Owen went away her partner was also away - I didn't have to be fully alone and she got it.".

Owen made 28 appearances for Plymouth Argyle last season.

Owen, now 27, has played most of his career in League One, with two stints in the Championship when we was with Blackpool and Oxford United.

Last season was spent on loan at Plymouth Argyle and he is currently a free agent - this means he is not tied to any club by a legal contract. Owen can now join a new team without a transfer fee because no former employer owns his registration rights.

Many of his moves have been on deadline day and he indicates he is "very aware of the sacrifices" his family make.

"There's always the risk that a move might not work," he states. "So I might uproot my whole family for this next venture and it all goes south.

"Over the years I've learned that until there's a contract signed on the dotted line, you could end up anywhere.".

Owen went on loan to Portsmouth in 2022 just days after Jessica gave birth to Xavier.

Owen returned to Blackpool the following year and made 32 appearances for the Tangerines.

The family moved to Bicester in 2024, as Owen helped Oxford United win promotion to the Championship.

Owen joined Wigan Athletic on loan the following year making his debut in a 2â1 FA Cup fourth-round defeat by Fulham.

Last season the family lived in Devon after Owen went on loan again - this time to Plymouth Argyle.

For now, Jessica's career in law is on hold, she instead has a job in social media and works from home.

She also posts about her experiences on TikTok, regularly using #wag and #waglife.

"My career can be picked up at any time - whereas his career is right now and you've really got to take every opportunity," she says.

"As much as people say it's a glamorous lifestyle you do make sacrifices so your partner can have their dream and get themselves as far as they can in football.

"At the end of the day, as much as I'm involved, it's his career. That means in order for me to support him properly I can't get emotionally involved.".

This includes not getting too emotionally attached to where they live.

"We usually rent newer houses that are a blank canvas so we can make them our own, although this last season the accommodation was provided furnished by Argyle," she states.

"We put a lot of Xavier's toys and garden stuff in storage and referred to our Plymouth accommodation as 'the holiday house'.

"It can be hard when he asks us to get things like his trampoline which we don't have with us.".

Owen's career is always the priority, Jessica says.

"When Owen was at Oxford he had one year left on his contract and I loved it there," she says.

"But the best thing was for him to go and get game time somewhere miles away. So we moved.".

While Premier League footballers can earn tens of thousands of pounds a week - sometimes hundreds of thousands - life in the lower leagues can be very different.

"When you think 'Wag' [players' wives and girlfriends] and you think 'footballer', both of those terms come with this stereotype that our lives are easy," Jessica says.

"People also put League One players in the same bracket as Premier League players.

"In the Premier League they're often set up for life - we can't live in that way because we have to prepare for life after football.".

Adding to the uncertainty of where they will be playing is also the possibility or relegation or injury.

Recent findings suggest that "When we were at Portsmouth, Blackpool was still his parent club and they got relegated," notes Jessica. "Owen wasn't even involved that season, but his wage was still affected.

Industry observers note that "You have to be prepared for everything. You just can't live outside of your means.

"But it's still a really fortunate position to be in.

Recent findings suggest that "Luckily, Owen's been good with injuries. There are some players who they get injured in the last month of the season and they're out of contract.

"In football things can be really positive or really negative.".

The uncertainty also affects their children - four-year-old Xavier and two-month old Etta.

"Now that Xavier is growing up - he's fast approaching school age - another thing that will have to be added into the mix is his stability," notes Jessica.

Even normal things like organising his recent fourth birthday party aren't always straightforward.

"We couldn't plan to have a party in Plymouth with balloons and cakes etc because we didn't know if we were going to be there," she claims.

"Instead we planned a party near my family in Stoke-on-Trent - we needed to make something work regardless of what happens with Owen's job.

"As much as I worry about Xavier and Etta, I also think how amazing it's going to be for them when they're older to be able to tell their life story and say they've lived in all these different places.

"I think it's teaching them a good life lesson that they don't need to be tied to one place.".

She claims they have made every move a positive experience.

"We've said to Xavier that we might be moving soon and when we do we're going to get his bike back out of storage," notes Jessica.

"That way he knows that moving is a possibility and hopefully he's not thinking about what he's going to lose but what he's going to gain.

"The fortunate thing for us is that Xavier loves football. He gets a lot of excitement as well from the new strips and the new chants and all of that kind of thing.".

Xavier has enjoyed watching his dad play at each of his new clubs.

So, does Jessica have any tips for people in a similar situation?

"The main thing for me personally - and what I've learned first hand - is the importance of keeping your own identity outside of football," she claims.

"If you get too wrapped up in it, it only puts more pressure on your partner.

"If you can get a hobby, a routine or even a work-from-home job, that can help - things that can move with you.".

Being sensible financially is also key.

"I'd also say that if you have a season where you get promoted, try not to change your lifestyle and to bank the promotion money so that you have as much stability as you can," she adds.

Industry observers note that "In our house, I de-clutter maybe once a month," she indicates. "This helps me because I don't have control over Owen's career. But what I do have control over is making sure that if and when anything does happen, the house is ready to be packed up and moved.

"When it's the transfer window I will proposal in one-week blocks - that gives me that little bit of certainty in a situation where I have no control.".

She admits "it can be hard" but "on the flip side it's so exciting".

In a recent development, "We've lived in places that we never would have lived in. And that's exciting for a relationship," she adds.

"You know, with some relationships you can get bored.

"In football, you don't get bored!".

Supporters of Israeli side Hapoel Beer-Sheva are expected to be permitted to travel for their Europa League fixture against Bournemouth in January.

A previous decision to ban fans of fellow Israeli team Maccabi Tel Aviv from a Europa League game at Aston Villa last November caused controversy, with the move openly denounced by the then Prime Minister, Sir Keir Starmer.

That call prompted an investigation by the Independent Office for Police Conduct in August into former West Midlands Police chief constable Craig Guildford over allegations of gross misconduct.

Presently, Dorset Police are planning on the basis that Hapoel travelling fans will attend the 28 January match, though security assessments and intelligence reviews remain ongoing with two months remaining before kick-off.

Dorset Police’s Gold Commander for the game, Assistance Chief Constable Lindsay Dudfield, stated: "We are continuing to work closely with partners to ensure we can facilitate a safe and enjoyable match for all concerned.

"As with previous fixtures, we regularly review the latest information and intelligence to inform our policing operation and the resources required. All intelligence received will be carefully verified before informing any decisions we make around our aims.

"We are also in regular contact with interested parties in our communities to ensure we communicate clearly with them around what to expect and our policing intends for the fixture, as well as listening to any concerns they may have.".

The match between Villa and Maccabi last year required the deployment of over 700 police officers.

Sources indicate that on Thursday, Hapoel’s encounter with Besiktas was interrupted following altercations involving police and supporters of the Turkish side. The fixture had been relocated to Georgia following recommendations from Turkish authorities, having originally been scheduled as a home game for Besiktas.

Reports indicated that Besiktas supporters displayed Palestinian flags alongside pro-Palestine banners before unrest broke out, forcing play to be stopped. Georgia’s interior ministry stated that 16 individuals were arrested and three officers suffered injuries.

The Turkish football federation described the actions of Georgian police towards Besiktas supporters as "unacceptable".

Denouncing the unrest and violence during the fixture, European football's governing body Uefa released a statement saying: "Violence, aggression, hatred and any form of provocative, discriminatory or extremist behaviour have no place in football.

In a recent development, "Uefa competitions are founded on the principles of respect, fair play, integrity and safety. The events witnessed at the above-mentioned matches run counter to these fundamental values and to Uefa’s objective, enshrined in its Statutes, of ensuring that football matches are played in a spirit of peace, mutual respect and sporting fairness.".

Uefa confirmed that an ethics and disciplinary inspector has been designated to investigate the incident.

73 goals from dropping deep - we ask Kane to break down how he did it

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Harry Kane is one of the leading names in the race for this year's Ballon d'Or, having scored 73 goals last season for club and country.
  • As Harry Kane's career has progressed, the 33-year-old has taken an increasingly complete role, popping up to collect the ball as deep as his own box.
  • Many wonder why a talisman tasked with scoring doesn't spend more time closer to goal, but last season the England and Bayern Munich striker scored 73 goals - the highest tally of his career - while playing deeper than he ever has done.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Harry Kane is one of the leading names in the race for this year's Ballon d'Or, having scored 73 goals last season for club and country.

As Harry Kane's career has progressed, the 33-year-old has taken an increasingly complete role, popping up to collect the ball as deep as his own box.

Many wonder why a talisman tasked with scoring doesn't spend more time closer to goal, but last season the England and Bayern Munich striker scored 73 goals - the highest tally of his career - while playing deeper than he ever has done.

When I mention this paradox, a grin spreads across his face.

"Until you really understand football and understand what we've been talking about, it's so easy to say 'stay high, you're going to score' but it doesn't work like that," Kane says.

I sat down to speak to Kane about the finer details of his game, shedding light on his unique role.

In a recent development, watching Kane train, his professionalism is palpable. England's record goalscorer is one of the first out on the pitch. The younger players indulge in playful kick-ups as he watches, engaged in conversation with a member of staff.

From a distance, that makes it easy to confuse him with a coach but, given his role on the pitch, it is a fitting mistake.

Kane's style of play reflects who he is as a person, with those who know him saying he is well-rounded and humble on and off the pitch.

How dropping deep helps Kane score.

It has been revealed that the season is in its infancy but Kane isn't basking in the success of the past 12 months. With only five days of pre-season training under his belt, the England captain completed 90 minutes of Bayern's 2-1 win over Borussia Dortmund to lift the German Super Cup.

As demanding as his roaming role is, he has taken the physical demands of it in his stride. Across the past six seasons, STATSports - a sports technology tech giant Kane has invested in - found his distance covered, high-speed running and accelerations were up 8%, 22% and 42% respectively.

And given how the tactical landscape has changed over that time, it is particularly impressive Kane has been able to not only keep up, but stay ahead.

Kane's role has evolved drastically over the past nine years, with the striker now heavily involved in all phases of the game -Â including as deep as his own box.

"Over the last five or six years, man-to-man pressure has become bigger," Kane indicates.

"European football is physical and top teams are trying to win the ball back high, trusting their defenders and midfielders to defend man for man to win their battles.".

Given that change, the best teams have recruited physical athletes and brilliant dribblers who can beat their man when the game becomes a series of one-against-ones.

Kane, not known for his dribbling - and by his own admission "not the fastest", has thrived on his own terms.

It has been revealed that against Dortmund, there was a specific moment Kane dropped deep, looking to arrive in space unmarked. Recognising the danger, two players converged on the Englishman.

Kane's dribbling is cerebral. His speed of thought provides him solutions to problems others would attempt to solve with their feet alone.

After getting low and using his strength to shrug centre-back Waldemar Anton off him, Kane rose, slightly adjusting his body to the right. These micro-adjustments are a hallmark of his game and through them he is able to shift an entire team's momentum.

Fooled by this feint, Daniel Svensson and Jobe Bellingham found themselves wrong-footed as Kane snapped the ball back the other way, opening up the entire pitch from within Bayern's half.

Kane wins his individual battle with Waldemar Anton, shielding the ball and showcasing strength.

As he rises, he positions his body to the right, facing his own goal.

Through clever body positioning, Kane moves the opposition towards the right side of the pitch. This is his cue to cut the ball back into the open space.

This allows Kane to evade two defenders, now facing the opposition's goal.

Earlier this year, Bayern boss Vincent Kompany shed light on Kane's unique role, explaining it as being 50% coached and 50% Kane deciding what to do.

"I think it's partly instinct, using my football brain and getting the feeling on the pitch," indicates Kane. "If, for example, I want to drop and see if the centre-back really wants to commit, he might commit into midfield, but is he going to commit if I drop all the way to my box?

"After the first five or 10 minutes you really get an understanding of how the opposition are going to play, which dictates how I play.".

Industry observers note that in the second minute of Bayern Munich's game against Arsenal, Kane dropped deep into a position normally occupied by centre-backs. Arsenal centre-back William Saliba marked him all the way, vacating space higher up the pitch.

There is a shared understanding at Bayern of an approach that allows team-mates to make sense of rotations that, to the naked eye, appear random.

Kane, who is given more freedom than most, is at the centre of it.

"I feel like my position now is as one of two 10s, and you work together," he says. "You can double up on one side to overload, which causes the opposition centre-backs a problem of who to mark.

"If they want to mark both, they've got to go man-to-man and then that leaves space for our wingers or full-backs to run into.

"It's posing all these questions to the opposition but, personally, I love having someone close to me who I can link with.".

Kane built his reputation playing as a lone number nine, so it is interesting to hear him identify instead as a number 10 -Â in a front two.

"When you're the number nine on your own you can get marked by two centre-backs and you struggle to get touches on the ball," he indicates. "You're relying on everyone else to find you with the ball.".

Showing Kane two clips from last season, I ask him to talk through what was going through his head.

According to recent reports, "The thing with our formation is, as long as there's someone in each position, it doesn't really matter who it is. Lucho [Luis Diaz] in this clip is playing as one of those 10s.

"I've come off to try and create a bit of space and Lucho's gone through the centre.".

Distracted by Kane's dropping-deep movement, one of the opposition midfielders is pulled towards him. This creates space, allowing Joshua Kimmich to punch the ball through to Diaz.

Recent findings suggest that "I think it's Serge [Gnabry] making the run in behind which takes the defenders back, which allows me and Lucho that space in between. Lucho lays it off and whenever I'm in that position, around 20-25 yards out, I'm always looking if I can get my shot off.".

It is one of many examples of Kane initially dropping deep before scoring.

In a recent development, "By playing deep when the play develops, I end up coming into a number 10 spot when everyone's dropped," he says. "I can get shots off from the edge of the box, which is a big strength of mine, or I'm running off the back of players where no-one's picking me up - because the midfielder finds it hard to [track].".

According to recent reports, the Frankfurt midfielder notices Kane dropping deep. Recognising this danger, he moves towards him.

Sources indicate that with Frankfurt's central midfielder pulled towards Kane, Luis Diaz is able to receive a pass between the lines. He forms a central front two with Kane. The wingers ahead of them, Serge Gnabry and Michael Olise, push the defensive line back.

Kane is found in space around the edge of the box and strikes the ball hard into the net.

The second clip is from Bayern's Champions League tie against Club Brugge.

Usually Kane is marked by an opposition centre-back, but the Belgian club give that responsibility to their holding midfielder -Â something he recognises and exploits.

Lennart Karl scores without Kane touching the ball, but the striker's involvement is undeniable.

"These are the little runs, again, not everyone sees," Kane explains. "With Jamal Musiala and Lenny, they're so good at receiving the ball and dribbling so there'll be times where I will actually stay higher and let those guys get on the ball a bit deeper, and I'll try and make runs in behind.

"Without changing my game too much, I try and complement the players around me.

"I know Lenny is so good in those pockets and when he gets there, I'm more thinking of running in behind because, one, he can play me in and I can go through on goal, or two, he can dribble with the ball and do exactly what happened here.

"As soon as Lenny gets in that pocket I make the run and not always to get the ball, sometimes it is just to drag the defender away.

"Now he's one-against-one with a centre-back in the middle of the pitch and that's dangerous for any centre-back.".

Karl receives the ball in the middle of the pitch. As seen in yellow, Kane is being marked by Club Brugge's holding midfielder, rather than any of the central defenders.

Kane, recognising this, makes a diagonal run in behind, pulling the opposition holding midfielder away from the centre of the pitch.

Karl drives with the ball into the space created by Kane before putting the ball into the top corner.

With the Ballon d'Or announcement on the horizon, Kane's name is in the conversation, primarily for the sheer volume of goals he has scored. What is easier to miss in that debate is the rest of his game.

Kane plays for the team in each phase of the game across the entirety of the pitch, while at the same time producing extraordinary individual numbers that match the likes of Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Erling Haaland.

He has described himself as playing in the role of a number 10, nine and six at times.

In a football world of specific and heavily drilled tactical roles, that is quite the achievement.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Panini have launched their latest Barclays Women's Super League sticker collection, featuring teams from WSL and WSL 2 for a second year running.

This is only the fourth edition of the book for the top women’s league in this country, and Rachel Daly believes the culture of sticker collecting can play its part in growing the women’s game.

As the latest collection was launched in London this week, the ex-Lioness spoke to FourFourTwo about the rise of the women's game.

Speaking at the launch, Daly reflected on her own childhood memories of collecting Panini stickers.

Industry observers note that "For me, it goes back to my childhood,” Daly told FourFourTwo. “I collected them with my brother. We used to, every Saturday morning, go and get the stickers.

"You'd get your piles and you'd trade them and swap them at school. Just that whole feeling of sitting down and putting stickers in.

"So to be in one is pretty cool.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

"I'm a Leeds fan, so I always wanted to get the whole Leeds team immediately when I was younger.

"I would literally swap any of my stickers, even if I'd already got the Leeds player, just to have more.”.

While Daly grew up collecting men’s players, this WSL collection offers an opportunity to introduce more fans to the women's game, something Daly believes is particularly notable as the league continues to grow.

The latest album has 545 stickers across all 26 WSL and WSL2 clubs, giving fans access to collect stickers of their favourite players from across the top two tiers of English women’s football.

"The visibility of the game is massive," she added.

"For the fact that it's WSL 1 and 2, I think it's equally as crucial. Those players in the WSL 2 deserve the same recognition as us.

"Being able to see kids being exposed to seeing the women's game as well, it's exciting.".

Sources indicate that daly was speaking at the launch of the Panini Barclays Women's Super League Official Sticker Collection 2027 in London. The collection is available now at retailers nationwide and online via Panini.co.uk.

She enjoys telling stories that capture the personalities, passion and excitement of the women’s game, on and off the pitch.
