💡 Key Takeaways
  • Going into the summer transfer window as Premier League champions, hope sprang eternal for Arsenal.
  • An opportunity to capitalise, encouraged by a sense at Emirates Stadium that their competitors were in transition because of managerial instability.
  • If ever there was a moment to strike in recruitment, this was it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Going into the summer transfer window as Premier League champions, hope sprang eternal for Arsenal.

An opportunity to capitalise, encouraged by a sense at Emirates Stadium that their competitors were in transition because of managerial instability.

If ever there was a moment to strike in recruitment, this was it.

According to recent reports, the prepares were ambitious: a shortlist with more than 20 players on it. They were targets at Real Madrid and Atletico Madrid, even at Chelsea and Tottenham.

But as the window shut on Tuesday night, you could not escape the sense of unfulfillment - certainly from a section of supporters.

Arsenal's close season was one characterised by some unquestionable successes, but also riddled by difficulties and frustration.

Ahead of their home match against Chelsea on Sunday, BBC Sport details Arsenal's transfer window and whether manager Mikel Arteta, sporting director Andrea Berta and, perhaps most pertinently, owners Kroenke Sports Entertainment can deem their summer operation a success.

Bruno Guimaraes's Â£75m capture from Newcastle United was Arsenal's most eye-catching signing.

Heading into the summer, Arsenal were keeping abreast of Guimaraes' situation at Newcastle, although others were considered a higher priority.

For instance, their interest in Elliot Anderson was widely reported, but it was clear the England international was joining Manchester City.

Guimaraes' former Newcastle team-mate Sandro Tonali and Bournemouth's Alex Scott were also among the midfielders explored before a move for the South American accelerated.

At the ages of 26 and 23 respectively, Tonali and Scott are younger than Guimaraes, who turns 29 in November.

But numerous factors, including availability and price - Tonali joined Spurs for a minimum Â£92m - made their signings difficult.

Aston Villa's Amadou Onana was also among the options considered, but the Belgium international suffered a serious knee injury at the World Cup.

By mid-June Guimaraes, who had universal backing inside the Emirates, emerged as the club's primary focus.

Berta knew the player's camp well and Guimaraes was admired by Arteta, who had made it clear he wanted proven talent to take his starting XI - rather than the wider squad - to greater heights.

Berta used his strong relationship with Guimaraes' representatives to facilitate Arsenal's move, hence why Newcastle maintained they had had no direct contact from the London club until days before his move was completed.

It is not uncommon for Berta to lean on intermediaries to conduct negotiations, although the approach has had varying degrees of success.

For instance, Arsenal actively sought moves for Leicester City teenagers Jeremy Monga and Louis Page over the summer.

But sources insist that the lack of club-to-club discussions meant both players ultimately did not join Arsenal, with Monga eventually signing for Manchester City when he appeared to be on the verge of moving to the Emirates.

That mentioned, Berta's success in pivoting the club towards a deal for Guimaraes when it became clear other targets were not viable was well received behind the scenes at Arsenal.

It has been revealed that the signing of Ezri Konsa was equally complex. Konsa was viewed internally as Arteta's first-choice defensive option.

Arteta wanted players used to the rigours of Premier League football - hence the moves for Guimaraes, Konsa and the failed efforts to land Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa.

Konsa's ability to play at right-back was also viewed as a major benefit. Arsenal considered signing an orthodox right-back, with Ivan Fresneda among the options, but Konsa's versatility was a key factor.

But Berta appeared reluctant to meet Villa's valuation. A week before the Konsa deal was confirmed, Arsenal made a Â£40m offer, which was duly rejected.

Sources claim the deal was eventually sealed by the ownership at both clubs, and the transfer was agreed at Â£51m, with Â£4m in add-ons.

In the event of not reaching an agreement for Konsa, it is understood Tottenham duo Cristian Romero and Micky van der Ven were identified as targets â but Arsenal's north London rivals would not consider selling to them.

Como centre-back Jacobo Ramon is a player the club will continue to monitor, but clauses attached to his current contract make the deal difficult.

Tarik Muharemovic, who joined Leeds United, was another considered.

In attack, Christos Tzolis' impact since arriving from Club Brugge in a deal worth about Â£35m means the Greece international has been heralded as one of the discoveries of the summer.

It is understood the potential deal for the former Norwich winger was initially raised by an intermediary close to a senior member of the coaching staff during the close season.

Berta's number two, Maurizio Micheli, watched Tzolis play for his country against Sweden in June and was suitably impressed.

So far, the 24-year-old looks a positive addition to Arteta's squad.

Arsenal, who also made Piero Hincapie's loan deal permanent and signed Illan Meslier on a free transfer, are happy with the signings they have made.

The captures of Guimaraes and Konsa, who will both be 30 by the end of next season, have raised eyebrows given the combined Â£126m fee, amid concerns over how the pair's longevity may impact the natural evolution of the squad.

Yet it is undeniable that Guimares and Konsa add elite quality and experience to Arsenal ranks, and ultimately the club feel they paid the going rate to get those deals over the line.

Vinicius Jr signed a new six-year deal at Real Madrid in August.

While the club delivered proven talent for Arteta in defence and midfield, Berta's remit of adding an elite attacker ended in disappointment.

Rogers was the club's primary target heading into the window, and the early indications were positive amid a strongly held view internally that the forward wanted to join.

At the start of the summer, it was Arsenal's understanding that Villa valued Rogers at Â£100m. Arsenal valued Rogers at Â£80m.

Berta, however, was confident of negotiating the price down to a level he and the club believed could get the deal done.

In the meantime, however, Berta explored alternatives - Bradley Barcola, Kenan Yildiz, Yan Diomande and Nico Paz were admired.

Anthony Gordon was a long-term target, but he had agreed before the World Cup to join Barcelona.

Yildiz and Paz will continue to be realistic targets moving forward. Eli Junior Kroupi is another the club will watch once he returns from injury for Bournemouth.

Anderson's move from Forest to City for Â£116m, however, altered the complexion of Villa's outlook on Rogers' future.

Villa increased their valuation to Â£120m and ultimately Chelsea ended up signing the attacker for Â£117m.

Arsenal, it is understood, were given the opportunity to match Chelsea's offer but refused, believing their Â£80m valuation was fair - but it does beg the question of whether Rogers would be a Gunners player now if Berta had acted sooner.

Ultimately, the failure to land Rogers arrived as the first of a series of blows to Berta in his efforts to deliver a top-class left-sided attacker for the team.

Arsenal genuinely believed they had a realistic chance of signing Vinicius Jr before he decided to sign a newly introduced contract at Real Madrid.

In a recent development, berta and Arteta were all in on the Brazil icon. The club were prepared finance the deal too.

While the transfer would likely have cost a British record fee and been one of the most lucrative remuneration packages in Premier League history, the benefit to Arteta's team and the Brazil superstar's commercial value meant Arsenal were absolutely prepared to complete the deal.

Yet well-placed sources expressed to BBC Sport over the summer that Vinicius did not want to leave Real, while others feared Arsenal were being used to strengthen the attacker's efforts to secure a more lucrative contract at the Bernabeu.

Those concerns came to fruition as Vinicius signed a new long-term contract in Spain in another Arsenal disappointment.

There were similar reservations about Arsenal's well-documented pursuit of Julian Alvarez.

The Atletico Madrid forward demonstrated very little indication that he was willing to join Arsenal; his preference to join Barcelona was one of the worst-kept secrets of the window.

But Atletico's point-blank refusal to sell to Barcelona was deemed reason enough by Berta and Arteta to persist with their interest in the hope of Alvarez changing his mind until the closing days of the window.

Alvarez, however, preferred to stay at Atletico, even though his relationship with the club is at an all-time low.

Recent findings suggest that did Arsenal waste their time with Vinicius and Alvarez? The answer varies depending on who you speak to.

When it became clear Alvarez was unlikely, Berta explored his options.

Intriguingly, Arsenal have admired Chelsea striker Joao Pedro, who was deemed not for sale over the summer, although there were concerns over how he would fit into Arteta's system.

It is claimed Berta relies significantly on his vast network of agent connections rather than acting on the club's existing scouting information when analysing the market.

For example, last summer, when all the scouting information pointed towards a move for Benjamin Sesko, Berta's arrival meant the club pivoted to Viktor Gyokeres, who is at the moment second-choice striker.

This summer the club's late dalliance with Lyon winger Malick Fofana provided a further example of Berta leaning on his agency connections after management agency Roc Nation offered Arsenal an opportunity to sign the Belgium international.

Berta's relationship with Roc Nation was particularly prevalent this summer given Arsenal's pursuit of Vinicius and the sale of Gabriel Martinelli, who are both clients of the agency.

It remains to be seen how much of an impact Arsenal's failure to sign a recognised top-level attacker impacts their season, particularly in light of Martinelli and Leandro Trossard's departures.

Arsenal headed into the window with a clear remit of ensuring the club become more sustainable and adept at trading.

Part of that directive is to ensure the club remain compliant with domestic and European financial regulations.

Depending on who you talk to, the size of the potential deals for Vinicius or Alvarez would have raised doubts over Arsenal's ability to stay within the regulations.

Nevertheless, ensuring they maximised the benefits of player trading will become an increasing part of Arsenal's financial operation in the future.

It has been revealed that there was already evidence of that through the sale of Martinelli, whose Â£60m exit to Al-Hilal was the club's record departure. Arsenal have also secured a sell-on clause in the deal.

The exits of Martinelli, Trossard, Gabriel Jesus, Christian Norgaard, Jakub Kiwior, Fabio Vieira and Karl Hein secured the club in the region of Â£114m.

Through intermediaries, a possible exit for Myles Lewis-Skelly was explored, with a fee of about Â£80m believed to have been mooted for the midfielder.

Manchester United, who were attracted to Lewis-Skelly's ability to play at left-back, were interested but ultimately deemed his valuation too high.

Of course, it is Berta's job to have a firm grasp on the level of interest in the club's players and their market value but, nevertheless, the thought of Lewis-Skelly's departure resulted in huge uproar from supporters.

As BBC Sport revealed last month, the Gunners resisted any temptation to sell Ethan Nwaneri on a permanent deal, the academy graduate landing a season-long loan deal to Borussia Dortmund that includes a January recall option if required.

The minimum Â£15m fee secured in Trossard's deal to Besiktas is also viewed as a good deal inside the Emirates given the Belgian turns 32 in December.

Having spent nearly Â£450m in 12 months, Berta's work in the market has helped the club deliver their first league title in 22 years.

Yet, despite the money splashed, there remain clear issues in the squad - certainly in attack.

The summer window has left many supporters questioning Berta's body of work at Arsenal.

And with the average age of the squad increasing following the captures of Konsa and Guimaraes, can the current options build a dynasty of success before the club need to spend heavily again on regenerating the team?

An in situ redox-converted molecule for all-perovskite tandem solar cells

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (583 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • All-perovskite tandem solar cells (TSCs) are gaining prominence due to their ability to surpass the efficiency limit of single-junction perovskite solar cells (PSCs)1,2.
  • This is a preview of subscription content, access via your institution.
  • Access Nature and 54 other Nature Portfolio journals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

All-perovskite tandem solar cells (TSCs) are gaining prominence due to their ability to surpass the efficiency limit of single-junction perovskite solar cells (PSCs)1,2. However, the efficiency and stability of all-perovskite TSCs are limited by chemical instability at the hole transport layer/perovskite interface in the tin-lead (Sn-Pb) narrow-bandgap subcell, which introduces deep trap states from tin cations and promotes non-radiative recombination3-5. Here we incorporate a redox-converted molecule of p-aminobenzohydrazide (ABH) into poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene):polystyrene sulfonate (PEDOT:PSS) that neutralizes PSS acidity, heals Sn4+ defects, and generates a dipole passivation effect upon oxidation. During the preparation of Sn-Pb perovskites, ABH suppresses interfacial oxidation by reducing Sn4+ defects and converts to p-aminobenzaldehyde (ABD), which suppresses photogenerated hole-induced Sn2+ oxidation, aligning energy levels for efficient hole extraction. The in situ redox-converted molecule stabilizes the buried interface during both device fabrication and operation, reduces non-radiative recombination and enhances stability. The resulting narrow-bandgap Sn-Pb PSC achieves a power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 25.4% (certified 25.2%) with an open-circuit voltage of 0.92 V and a fill factor of 83.4%. Integrated into monolithic all-perovskite TSCs, the device delivers a PCE of 31.1% (certified 30.8%) together with enhanced thermal (ISOS-D-2I, 85 °C) and operational stability (ISOS-L-1I) under inert conditions.

Latest Update: Arsenal's tifo for crunch clash with Man City will NOT mention Premier League guilty verdict as insiders lift lid on plans for fresh design ahead of Emirates contest

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1326 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 16:30 EST, 26 November 2026 | Updated: 10:13 EST, 27 November 2026.
  • Industry observers note that tifos are back at the Emirates.
  • An emotionally-charged fixture between the title holders and the team found guilty of the majority of 115 breaches of the league's financial rules by an independent commission (which is being appealed by Man City) awaits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 16:30 EST, 26 November 2026 | Updated: 10:13 EST, 27 November 2026.

Industry observers note that tifos are back at the Emirates. Those loud, passionate designs which last season galvanised Arsenal en route to a first Premier League title in 22 years return on Sunday for the visit of Manchester City.

An emotionally-charged fixture between the title holders and the team found guilty of the majority of 115 breaches of the league's financial rules by an independent commission (which is being appealed by Man City) awaits.

Still, it can be revealed that Sunday's display will be more restrained than initially considered.

In a recent development, daily Mail Sport understands that a supporter-led group, established by the Arsenal Advisory Board (AAB) last season, initially raised an idea with Arsenal of referencing Man City's charges in the tifo. However, following consultation with the club, collectively the idea was dropped.

Instead the tifo will be done 'in the Arsenal way to inspire the fanbase', a source says. They added: 'It will galvanise and charge the fans in the right way.'.

These matters can often be delicate. For example, it's understood a debate was had over the north London derby tifo ahead of Arsenal vs Tottenham in November 2025 at the Emirates, which involved a montage of club icons from past and present. And at the very top, positioned deliberately, sat Sol Campbell.

Sol Campbell, perched atop this Arsenal tifo for the derby game against Tottenham last season, moved between the clubs in a highly contentious transfer in 2001.

What Arsenal offered on that PSG night in 2025 caused embarrassment – a solitary white cannon on a red backdrop.

Industry observers note that his 2001 move from Spurs to the Gunners remains one of the rivalry's deepest fault lines. Arsenal initially thought it could be too provocative but proceeded as the group were adamant on the imagery.

The reception when the tifo unveiled was immediate. The players felt it. The supporters felt it. Thierry Henry himself shared the image on social media with a simple verdict: 'What a tifo! Thank you, Gooners!'.

As revealed in the book 22 Years: The Inside Story of Arsenal's Title-Winning Season, later in the season Mikel Arteta met up with the creators to say thank you and gifted each of them a signed, framed picture of the Tottenham tifo. Stuart MacFarlane, the club's chief photographer, was also there to take pictures of the group alongside Arteta. The Spaniard privately values the energy these displays create and embraces them.

Sources indicate that it's understood Arteta checks the tifo designs before they are finalised. Much work goes into creating them, as reflected in the final proposal for Sunday's tifo which had to be confirmed and sent to the manufacturers nearly three weeks before matchday.

In a recent development, the artwork is printed on a square shape canvas which is then cut out and backed onto a paper-like material. That is cable-tied to a huge rectangular netting and tied to the roof with further cables and ropes.

In a recent development, the design along with the attached apparatus weighs around a couple of hundred kilograms, which is a serious amount. The lightweight fabric also has to be fire retardant and meet weight restrictions.

The work involved in putting the tifo together has seen volunteers invited to the Hale End academy this Friday to cable tie the tifo and get the design laid out on an indoor pitch.

Budgets have to be met, too, for the group are allocated an undisclosed amount to cover tifos for the whole season. Blowing the budget on one or two displays would rule out further spectacles later in the season.

According to recent reports, the latest design builds on a growing trend which Arsenal began to grasp just over a year ago, the mission to properly create tifos initially starting in April 2025. Arsenal had unveiled their own tifo ahead of a Champions League semi-final first leg against Paris Saint-Germain — the first to be draped from the Emirates Stadium's roof in the arena's history.

For those confused by the term 'tifo', it stems from the Italian word tifosi, meaning passionate supporters. The designs are an attempt to galvanise fans, building an atmosphere with powerful messaging and provocative imagery to unsettle opponents.

Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta checks the tifo designs before they are unveiled.

Mikel Arteta stated he hopes Manchester City's guilty verdict for breaching Premier League financial rules does not overshadow Sunday's crunch clash against Arsenal.

Recent findings suggest that man City were found guilty of the large majority of charges for breaking the league's financial regulations between 2009 and 2018, in a period which saw them win eight trophies. The Manchester club insist they're innocent and are appealing the independent commission's verdict.

When asked about whether the charges will overshadow the match, Arteta stated: 'I hope that it doesn't because it's a process that is still open, it's not resolved and I don't know what is going to happen.

'I think when we have two teams at the level that they both are at right now with the quality players that are on that pitch, it's a massive game and a significant game to enjoy.'.

Sources indicate that he added: 'That (the match) is the only thing that we should put the energy and the focus in. There's nothing else.'.

Meanwhile, Arteta said there is a chance David Raya will be fit enough to play on Sunday.

Raya appeared to be in agony as he was forced off in the 70th minute of Arsenal's 2-2 draw at Newcastle last Saturday, hurting his left shoulder in an accidental collision with William Osula.

There were initial fears the goalkeeper could be facing an extended spell on the sidelines, with Kepa Arrizabalaga playing in Tuesday's Champions League match against Borussia Dortmund.

Arteta said: 'We still have a few hours before the game. We're still trying to get everyone back.'.

On if there's 'a ray of hope' that Raya will be available, he added: 'Yeah.'.

What Arsenal offered on that PSG night was widely mocked – a solitary white cannon on a red backdrop. That was it. A sterile design for one of the biggest European nights the Emirates had ever hosted, at that time.

It's understood a club-produced design had been used over a fan-led alternative, mainly because there was limited time between the proposal and the game itself.

The episode proved to be a pivotal turning point, led by the AAB.

It has been revealed that the AAB is the club's formal fan-engagement body, created in 2021 following the backlash over Arsenal's involvement in the wretched European Super League plot — a breakaway competition set to feature 12 of Europe's leading clubs. The subsequent supporter anger forced Arsenal to improve their communication with fans.

After the PSG tifo disappointment, the AAB helped create a newly introduced group for the start of the 2025–26 season focused on creating tifos. Arsenal wanted to learn from the error, and this was their way of putting fans back in control.

It's worked. The outcome resulted in a slew of eye-catching displays in the previous campaign from Campbell to Leandro Trossard's eye-goggles celebration for the 'history in our sights' tifo ahead of the Champions League quarter-final second leg against Sporting Lisbon — or the 'over land and sea' design with a huge ship for the semi-final second leg against Atletico Madrid.

By softening the parameters and letting fan representatives into the inner sanctum, Arsenal have utilised a marginal gain Arteta had craved ever since he took charge seven years ago — make the Emirates a fortress.

While there was an initial temptation from the AAB to reference Man City's guilty verdict in Sunday's tifo, the overall message will be unmistakably clear: Arsenal are now in charge.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

US and UK to host Women's World Cups in 2031 and 2035

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (370 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • FIFA have confirmed the hosts for the 2031 and 2035 Women's World Cup.
  • According to recent reports, the United States, along with Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica, made an uncontested bid to host in 2031.
  • Recent findings suggest that FIFA's revenue for the 2026 men's World Cup was around $15 billion (€13.7 billion), and it's clear that US Soccer feels that hosting the women's tournament is the next move forward.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

FIFA have confirmed the hosts for the 2031 and 2035 Women's World Cup.

According to recent reports, the United States, along with Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica, made an uncontested bid to host in 2031. It will be the first tournament to feature 48 teams — as is the case with the men. The US has hosted the event twice before, in 2003 and 1999, and is also the most successful country in its history, having won it four times.

Recent findings suggest that FIFA's revenue for the 2026 men's World Cup was around $15 billion (€13.7 billion), and it's clear that US Soccer feels that hosting the women's tournament is the next move forward. With the women's domestic league (NWSL) considered the strongest in the world and the US national team so dominant, securing the tournament in 2031 is a further sign of the US' committment to women's football.

"We expect and plan for the 2031 Women’s World Cup to be the largest women’s sporting event in history," Emily Cosler, US Soccer’s vice-president of strategy told The Guardian.

It has been revealed that the 2035 tournament was also awarded to the sole bidders, England, Scotland, Northern Ireland and Wales. This sees the World Cup return to the United Kingdom for the first time since 1966, the only time England's men's team won the competition. The women lost the 2023 final to Spain. It also means that the UK will host two major tournaments in relatively quick succession, with the men's 2028 European Championships also set to be held in England, Scotland and Wales and the Republic of Ireland.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the tournament would bring "visitors, investment and jobs to every part of the country.".

Given that FIFA President Gianni Infantino had revealed last year that both bids were unchallenged, this news comes as little surprise. Nevertheless, with the hosts now official, a 48-team tournament marks a remarkable advance for the women's game. The 2011 World Cup in Germany had just 16 teams.

The next World Cup will be in Brazil in 2027, running from June 24 to July 25. . Eighteen of the 32 teams have already secured qualification, including Germany.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It was, claims Ido Rakovsky, like reporting on "science fiction", rather than sport.

Israel, whose senior team have qualified for the World Cup just once, had beaten global powerhouses Brazil in the quarter-finals of the under-20 version of the tournament.

At the final whistle, the commentator covering the match for Israeli television vowed "you will tell of this night to your children, and they will tell it to your grandchildren".

Five days later, the team's semi-final against Uruguay was the most-watched thing of the evening on Israeli television, drawing a 23% viewing share.

Politicians clamoured to congratulate the team.

"That summer, everybody was watching under-20 football, everybody knew the players," says Rakovsky, who was covering the team for Israeli media outlet Haaretz.

"Everybody in Israel fell in love with these kids.".

It wasn't just their deeds on the pitch that felt otherworldly, though.

After scoring a stoppage-time winner against Uzbekistan in the last 16, Anan Khalaili had given an interview to Israeli television.

In it Khalaili, an Israeli Arab, thanked the viewers back home for staying up late to watch his team win in Argentina.

To do so, he used the words 'Am Yisrael' - a Hebrew phrase that means 'People of Israel' and is bound up in Jewish religion, community, culture and history.

"That an Arab player used that figure of speech mentioned something about the identity of that team," says Rakovsky.

"That team made real the claim that football can really bring people together - that Muslim players are part of the national team of the Jewish state, representing Israel and creating something better, both for the present and future.".

But a little over four months after Khalaili's interview and the win over Brazil, Hamas attacked Israel.

Recent findings suggest that the armed Palestinian group killed about 1,200 people and took 251 hostages. In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza. The United Nations believes the retaliation has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians., external.

As the war goes on, can the potential of a golden generation of Israel's footballers, in sport and society, be realised?

Israel beat Brazil 3-2 in the quarter-finals of the U20 World Cup in 2023.

Beaten 1-0 by eventual champions Uruguay, Israel finished third at that Under-20 World Cup in 2023.

The same set of players, with a few additions and omissions, had already impressed at continental level.

They were runners-up at 2022's Under-19 Euros, beaten by England in extra-time in the final, and would go on to make the semi-finals of 2023's Under-20 Euros.

Israel has produced outstanding players in the past. Eyal Berkovic and Yossi Benayoun were technical, gifted attackers with long Premier League careers.

But a depth of talent, emerging together, sets the current cohort apart.

Khalaili has been one of the most sought-after young prospects in Europe this summer.

After his Â£21.5m move to Inter Milan fell through, Crystal Palace saw off competition from Nottingham Forest to pick him up for a similar fee from Belgian side Union Saint-Gilloise.

Playmaker Oscar Gloukh, 22, wears Ajax's number 10 shirt after his form earned a move from Red Bull Salzburg.

Left-back Roy Revivo signed for Spanish club Elche on transfer deadline day this month from Maccabi Tel Aviv, while Twente defender Stav Lemkin, also 23, is also highly rated.

Dor Turgeman, Ilay Feingold and Idan Toklomati are impressing in Major League Soccer in the United States.

All have now won full caps, but were moulded into a collective, cohesive unit - something that has often been beyond the senior side - by Israel's age-grade coach Ofir Haim.

"It isn't an glitch at all here," Haim said, external of the different backgrounds in his squad during the 2023 Under-20 World Cup.

In a recent development, "We don't have any problem with religion. Not at all. We have players here who put on tefillin [Jewish ceremonial wear, containing verses from the Torah] - and Anan [Khalaili], Hamza [Shibli] and Ahmed [Salman] perform the Muslim prayers.

In a recent development, "We don't even talk about this. We unite everybody, and I wish the country were as united as this team.".

Ofir Haim managed various domestic teams in Israel before becoming head coach of the U19s and U20s.

Football has long been the part of Israeli society where communities mix together who may not otherwise meet.

"The majority of the Jewish people who arrived in the mandate period [a spell between 1923 and 1948 where the region was run by Britain] emigrated from Europe," says Dr Omer Einav, a historian and author of Defending the Goal, a book on Israel's football history.

Recent findings suggest that "They were Europeans and when you think about cinema, music, theatre, dance, they had nothing in common with Middle Eastern culture. Nothing, except football. That was the only common language, the only thing they both love in the same way.".

Encouraged by the British administrators who ran the region, teams from different communities, and some made up of elements of each, would play against each other.

In a recent development, when the modern state of Israel was formed in 1948, much of the Arab population that remained inside its borders continued to identify as or with Palestinians. Most still do.

They are also an intrinsic part of Israeli football.

While they make up 20% of Israel's population, they represent about 35% of those involved in the sport at elite level nationally.

The first Arab player to represent Israel's national team was Rifaat Turk in 1976. In 2018, Bibars Natcho became the first Muslim to captain the team.

Neither was without controversy.

Turk was roundly abused. Natcho's decision not to sing Israel's national anthem, the lyrics of which relate to the Jewish search for a homeland, was condemned by some., external.

For a short time in the summer of 2023, it seemed as if Haim's under-20 side might offer a watershed moment of unity and co-existence.

But football, like everything in Israel, changed on 7 October.

Israel came second in their group at the U20 World Cup and went on to finish third in the tournament.

Matan Segal directed Kick It Out Israel, an anti-discrimination initiative with similar aims but no link to the English organisation of the same name, for almost four years before stepping down a few months ago.

In a recent development, racism has long been present in Israeli club football. Beitar Jerusalem's fans are among the most notorious.

In 2013, ultras burned down their own club's offices in protest at the signing of two Chechen Muslims.

The most extreme Beitar fans have long taunted Israeli Arabs with chants of "may your village burn", while declaring themselves "forever pure".

However during his time at Kick It Out Israel, Segal saw racism against Arab players become more virulent and widespread.

Covid, during which fans radicalised online during lockdown, was one cause.

The election of Israel's far-right government at the end of 2022, legitimising views towards Palestinians that were previously seen as extreme, was a second.

The war was undoubtedly another.

"Before 7 October, people generally respected the Arab players," Segal said.

"Even though they had difficulties with them not singing the Israeli anthem, they respected them and they could talk about it.

"After 7 October though, we saw an increase in racist remarks.

Recent findings suggest that "It was happening at small clubs where we hadn't seen it before. There were terrible songs - 'Let's kill all Arabs', 'There are no schools in Gaza because there are no children left'.".

Football, inevitably, has become a focal point for emotion generated by the conflict.

Recent findings suggest that clubs which are usually bitter rivals came together to remember those killed by Hamas. Scarves were part of the commemoration at the site of the Nova music festival, where hundreds were killed.

Hapoel Jerusalem's club badge now features a silhouette of Hersh Goldberg-Polin, who was abducted and killed in captivity and whose parents have campaigned for peace through their grief.

Meanwhile, Israeli Defence Force (IDF) soldiers have posed with club flags and banners while on operation in Gaza, dedicating their actions to the clubs and ultras back home., external.

In such a heightened atmosphere, young footballers â closely connected to the conflict through Israel's programme of national service and a barrage of online commentary and images â are under constant scrutiny and pressure.

Gloukh's lifelong friend Afik Tery was killed by a Hamas explosive while serving in the IDF.

After his death, Gloukh posted a poignant set of pictures, external of the pair arm-in-arm over time - as young boys at birthday parties, as young men at a wedding - with the final slide showing Tery's funeral.

Among the online replies were the taunts of pro-Palestinians.

For Israel players with Palestinian heritage, the stakes are especially and dangerously high.

According to recent reports, dia Saba plays in a similar playmaking role to Gloukh. The 33-year-old has scored three goals in 13 appearances for Israel.

He is unlikely ever to add to that tally.

Saba was one of Maccabi Haifa's most high-profile stars when, at the start of the conflict, his wife Narmin posted a message to Instagram.

"There are children in Gaza, too," she wrote.

In a recent development, saba apologised for the outrage caused, but could not save his career in Israel. He left Maccabi Haifa in 2025 and now plays for Turkish side Amedspor.

"My dream was to play for Maccabi Haifa, the club that I support, the team that I grew up with," Saba mentioned at the time.

In a recent development, "I wanted to continue. But sometimes there are reasons that are stronger than us that don't allow it.".

Former Israel Under-21 player Ataa Jaber (right) switched nationalities to represent Palestine in June 2023.

Saba and others are used to having their loyalty questioned. From all sides.

Many in the Arab world would like more Palestinian prospects within Israel to follow the example of Ataa Jaber.

Jaber captained Israel's Under-21 side but switched nationalities, external to represent Palestine in June 2023, saying he could no longer separate sport and politics after seeing police evict Palestinian families from their homes in Israeli-occupied East Jerusalem.

Recent findings suggest that switching away from a high level of international football damaged his prospects of a move to Europe. At home, there were calls for his Israeli citizenship to be revoked. But, for Jaber, it was preferable to representing a country whose actions he deplored.

Those footballers who voice an opinion on the conflict choose their words carefully.

Beram Kayal, the former Brighton, Celtic and Israel player, knows the dilemmas and reality well.

Sources indicate that "To be Arabic in Israel, it's sometimes hard," he indicates. "Sometimes it is tough.

"Opportunities-wise, sometimes we are not on the same level.".

However, he believes in a pluralistic future for Israel and football as a tool to achieve it.

His friendship with Tomer Hemed - whom he first met as a young teenager at Maccabi Haifa's academy and later played alongside at Brighton and Charlton, as well as international level - sums up his approach.

"When I played with Tomer, he prayed like this," he says, touching his hand to his back of his head to indicate a kippah, the small skullcap worn as a sign of Jewish faith.

"And I was praying for Allah," he adds, raising his arms above his shoulders in worship.

"He was my team-mate and he is my brother.

It has been revealed that "In football, on the pitch, you never look at colour, culture or religion. You just want the best people around you to win the game.".

The 38-year-old is now employed by Israel's Football Association to work with young talents from Palestinian areas.

In doing so he works alongside former Israel goalkeeper Boni Ginzburg, who played across Glasgow at Rangers and is now the IFA's technical director.

After Arabic was relegated behind Hebrew as Israel's official language by a controversial 2018 law promoted by prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the IFA put on Hebrew language lessons for Arabic-speaking coaches to ensure they could still obtain their qualifications.

"Not in our building," claims Kayal when asked about the precedence given to Hebrew.

"I'm in this place [the IFA] to bring the culture of the Arabic people to the table.

"I say to the Arabic players when they come into the national team: Speak in your language, don't be afraid, don't be shy to speak, don't just afraid to show yourself.

Recent findings suggest that "Israel is a young country. We need to learn from our DNA, to see the different between the Jewish, the Circassians, the Arabic, the Muslim, the Christian, the Druze â all the colours â put that together and learn what we could do better.".

Israel are aiming to qualify for Euro 2028.

Israel's aim is to go better than their national team has managed in more than 50 years.

Sources indicate that ran Ben-Shimon was appointed as the senior side's head coach in 2024. He was given the goal of converting youthful promise into qualification for Euro 2028, which will be staged in England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland.

Success would place more stress on Israel's players and, potentially, squad unity.

Large-scale protests are planned for Republic of Ireland's forthcoming Nations League matches with Israel. Dublin will host seven games at the tournament.

Villa Park in Birmingham, from which Maccabi Tel Aviv fans were banned from attending a Europa League match in November, will stage four matches.

Hampden Park, two miles across Glasgow from where Celtic fans have held vociferous pro-Palestine protests, has six.

Wherever Israel play, players will be confronted with criticism of their country's treatment of Palestinians, both at home and in Gaza, that is rarely voiced at home.

"Israelis are very sensitive to anyone showing any kind of sympathy for what happened on 7 October," claims Dr Sophia Solomon, part of Ben-Gurion University's Center for Sports Diplomacy.

According to recent reports, "It is like denying the Holocaust, that is the proportion of it. A war is a special situation, it wasn't like this before, but to express your agony became more encouraged as we saw the European arena become more anti-Israeli.

"One reaction ignited another and there is more obligation to identify yourself with the victims of 7 October.".

She believes that it will take time for Israeli society, footballers included, to understand the past three years and speak openly about the conflict.

Industry observers note that "Until the ongoing war ends, no-one can say what he thinks," she stated. "Even after the Middle East returns to its 'normal' craziness, maybe it will take a decade to pass before people can start talking about their experiences and expectations.

"Time has to pass until you can touch certain areas, and at the moment you can see a lot of avoidance about talking about it, even mentioning it.".

Anan Khalaili, who scored in Israel's Under-20 World Cup victory over Brazil in 2023, joined Crystal Palace this summer.

The time for this stellar generation to fulfil their potential may come before that.

It may not. Translating youth-level promise to senior-level product is never simple.

But, whatever the future holds, for a few months, in the summer of 2023, Haim and his team gave Israel something special.

"We saw Anan Khalaili and Hamza Shibli scoring against Brazil and that was our hope, that was the future. That was our future," claims Einav.

"I'm not so optimistic, but people thought maybe it's really a magical thing that can help Israeli society in general.

"There was something there, something latest, something where people mentioned 'OK, if we co-operate, if we work together, we can also succeed in sport.'.

Industry observers note that "That's what we all care about, right? We want to be good at sports. We are sick of watching the World Cup from our living room.

"I think football is in some isolated, sterilised dimension - some kind of bubble - inside Israeli society. It is not hermetic. A lot of dirt comes in - racism, violence - but I do believe that football can reflect good things that can happen. The equality of chances, the tolerance and solidarity of all people living here.

"It can't heal anything but it can help us see one another in a more human way.

"So, yeah there was definitely a moment, but it was before our world changed and collapsed.".

Only time will tell what remains of that moment and whether it can be revived.

Ingvar Jonsson, the former Iceland goalkeeper who was part of the squad that defeated England at the 2016 European Championship, has died at the age of 37.

In a recent development, his former club Víkingur announced his death on Thursday. The team did not provide a cause of death, although Jonsson had reportedly been diagnosed with cancer earlier this year.

In a statement, the Icelandic club mentioned: "It is with great sorrow and deep sadness that we announce that our dear friend and teammate Ingvar Jonsson, goalkeeper for Víkingur, passed away on Wednesday, November 25, in the arms of his loved ones.".

It has been revealed that they added: "The club and all of Víkingur are thinking of his family and loved ones. We send them our deepest condolences.".

Industry observers note that jonsson served as an unused substitute during Euro 2016, when Iceland created one of the greatest shocks in tournament history by knocking England out in the round of 16. The team were later eliminated by France in the quarter-finals.

Industry observers note that paying tribute on X, European football’s governing body Uefa wrote: "We extend our deepest condolences to Ingvar’s family, friends and former team-mates. Our thoughts are with them at this difficult time.".

According to recent reports, jonsson earned eight international caps for Iceland, having made his first squad back in 2012. He had to wait another two years before making his first appearance for his country in a friendly against Belgium.

His final cap for Iceland came in 2019, but he continued to make the squad through until 2022.

His club career saw him start at Njardvik in his homeland before moving to Norwegian outfit IK Start in 2015. He would go on to play for Sandnes Ulf and Sandefjord prior to leaving Norway in 2018 to join Danish side Viborg.

After two years in Denmark, Jonsson returned to Iceland to play for Vikingur and remained at the club until his passing.

The part-timers who won three Wembley finals in a row

📅 30 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2024 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Question: Which two men's club sides have won three successive competition finals at the fresh Wembley?
  • You probably knew Pep Guardiola's Manchester City won three League Cups on the bounce between 2018 and 2020 before adding a fourth in 2021 â but another side did the silverware hat-trick first.
  • Whitley Bay, who play in the ninth-tier Northern Football League, won three successive FA Vase finals between 2009 and 2011 â an unprecedented achievement in non-league football.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Question: Which two men's club sides have won three successive competition finals at the fresh Wembley?

You probably knew Pep Guardiola's Manchester City won three League Cups on the bounce between 2018 and 2020 before adding a fourth in 2021 â but another side did the silverware hat-trick first.

Whitley Bay, who play in the ninth-tier Northern Football League, won three successive FA Vase finals between 2009 and 2011 â an unprecedented achievement in non-league football.

The FA Vase, a national competition for amateur teams, was established in 1974; and in more than half a century The Seahorses are the only ones to win it four times â including those three on the trot.

And they did so under the eye of an unassuming IT manager from Sunderland, who used "quiet moments in the day" to plan historic cup success.

Ian Chandler, who had three spells at Whitley Bay as a player, became manager in 2004 and spent 10 years in charge.

It was no mean feat, as any non-league manager will tell you. Instead of focusing on work meetings, Chandler notes he spent more time sorting hotel bookings or discussing scouting reports.

According to recent reports, his team were inspired by missing out on Wembley in 2007-08, when Whitley Bay reached the FA Vase semi-finals. They lost 4-0 to Lowestoft Town in the first leg, and despite going 3-0 up inside 20 minutes of the return fixture at Bay's Hillheads Park stadium they were unable to overturn the deficit.

After that elimination, Chandler developed a superstition of never again giving pre-match interviews - as the last time he did so was before the 4-0 defeat.

Whether because of his renewed focus, or because of a desire among players to make amends, it steeled the group to make history.

"It's the hardest thing to keep a team together - as soon as players get noticed, they get picked up at higher level," Chandler tells BBC Sport.

"But after we got to the Vase semis, players wanted to stay and prove what they could do.

"Then the lads wanted to do it again.".

Ian Chandler played for Barnsley, Stockport and Aldershot before a successful non-league career.

Despite being a lifelong Sunderland fan, Chandler admits basing his team on Kevin Keegan's Newcastle - with entertainment even placed above winning.

It has been revealed that "There was a standing joke in the team, two or three at the back? One time we chased a game with two at the back," he indicates.

"The Premier League can be so boring; fans want to be entertained, that's what we promised.".

Chandler was already a Whitley Bay hero when he was appointed manager by chairman Paul McIlduff, having scored the winner in the 2002 FA Vase final against Tiptree United at Villa Park.

After a slow start as the then-35-year-old with no prior managerial experience found his bearings, Chandler built a talented team which became the envy of non-league football nationwide.

Recent findings suggest that "We played good football. We had pace on the wing, fantastic midfielders, and strikers who were deadly," indicates McIlduff, who has been Whitley Bay chairman since 2001.

"When we brought them in, it was about fitting the psychology of the dressing room. No-one thought they were better than anyone else, they played for each other.".

A growing influence in the side was the 'Whitley Bay Maradona'.

Paul Robinson came through Newcastle United's academy before a career spent across various non-league clubs in the north-east â including Whitley Bay from 2007 to 2013.

Like several other players and staff, he worked with Chandler both in his day job at software organization Sage and at Hillheads Park.

In a recent development, "He was my manager at work and football, I was sick of him," he tells BBC Sport. "But it helped get time off for matches.".

And it meant he also had an understanding boss if his mind drifted at work.

"Zoning out happened regularly, picturing scoring and winning, what the opposition would be like - hoping they were rubbish so we could have an easy stroll," he indicates.

Perhaps Robinson's greatest Whitley Bay moment came in the 2010 FA Vase semi-final second leg, when his last-minute diving header in the driving rain secured a 6-5 aggregate victory over Barwell, sparking a pitch invasion.

"Everyone goes to the finals, you were there, you could enjoy it," notes Robinson, who is now academy head at South Shields.

"But the rounds before were the bigger games. At home, we would get 2,000 or 3,000 at every game. You felt like a real player. You associate those memories with 90s FA Cup you never think it will happen in non-league.".

Chandler played in a 2-0 win over Preston in round two as they reached the FA Cup third round for the first and only time in the 1989-90 season, and they also progressed to round two the following campaign.

Those seasons of success - made The Bay a feared side for non-league clubs across England, and meant they were ready for the major games in a way most amateur sides are not.

Industry observers note that "One quarter-final against Biggleswade [in 2009], they turned up in suits and ties," claims Robinson. "We thought, this is their day out, their cup final. We won 5-2.

Industry observers note that "By the end, teams were turning up afraid of us. We had it won beforehand.".

Paul Robinson scored the fifth goal in Whitley Bay's 6-1 win over Wroxham in the 2010 FA Vase final.

Recent findings suggest that off the pitch, the team's success had an influence on the whole of Whitley Bay. A working-class town near Newcastle, which had its heyday as a Victorian-era holiday destination, sporting success brought local pride to the north-east coast.

And like any lower league club, that success could only be supported by dedicated volunteers, who went into overdrive before the Vase finals.

They would go door to door across shops in Tynemouth, North Shields and Whitley Bay to raise support. A van selling tickets was parked outside Woolworths on the high street.

"There was such excitement around the whole of Whitley Bay - every shop had things in the windows, the blue and white stripes," claims one of the volunteers, Jenn Robinson.

She got involved because her late husband Mike was a club board member and if she wanted to see him she "had to go around there".

"Everyone wanted to come and watch, we got so many local sponsors," adds Jenn.

"I still do buffets and things for players and long-standing fans. We have a game tonight, and I'm making the sandwiches now.".

Newcastle United helped out with selling tickets for the finals, while North Tyneside Council provided security services as thousands flocked to Hillheads Park for big cup games.

But even the best laid aims can go awry.

"We organised a train down to London, the guarantee was that it would go straight to Wembley," says McIlduff. "The first time it worked, second time they were taken to Kings Cross - we had to organise taxis up to Wembley.".

By hook or by crook, The Seahorses army made it three times to the national stadium. Some even got royal treatment.

In a recent development, "It was absolutely surreal, and a delight," Jenn says. "The first Wembley final we played at, it had just opened. My husband being on the board, we sat in the royal box, which was fabulous.

In a recent development, "One of the security guys showing me to our seats said, 'Miss Robinson, this is Prince William's seat'. He hadn't even sat in it at that point.".

Thousands of fans travelled from Whitley Bay to London across the three finals.

Chandler, whose son Benjamin was a mascot at all three finals, said it was an overwhelming experience at times for the players too.

"The first year was crazy, everything was brand new," he claims. "The first year the bus driver scraped the side up of the bus driving into the ground.

"The second year we tried to take everything in, all the lads had their mobiles. Then the third year, it was just a case of can we do it, win three in a row.".

And three times, Whitley Bay rose to the occasion.

After beating Glossop North End 2-0 in 2009 in front of 12,200 supporters, Whitley Bay returned a year later to thrash Wroxham 6-1.

Recent findings suggest that the opening goal was scored by prolific striker Paul Chow after only 21 seconds. At the time this was the quickest goal in a Wembley final and was only surpassed 13 years later when Ilkay Gundogan scored for Manchester City inside 13 seconds in the FA Cup final.

The hat-trick was completed in 2011 with a frantic 3-2 win over Coalville Town, who equalised twice before Chow was again the hero with an 86th-minute winner.

In total, nearly 30,000 fans were in the stands across the three finals.

After each final, Whitley Bay celebrated in The Green Man pub just 15 minutes' walk from the famous Wembley arch.

In a recent development, "In the first year we just went back to the bar and it was an anti-climax," Robinson says. "The second and third years the club got their act together and we rented a room; families, friends and fans were invited, they were brilliant nights.

In a recent development, "In 2010, we actually spent 10 days together - the week of the final we spent as a squad preparing, then we went to Marbella for five nights. Best 10 days of my life!".

According to recent reports, the 2010 trophy lift was perhaps the most emotional though, as the players were joined by former team-mate Mark Taylor. He had played in the previous year's final, before being diagnosed with motor neurone disease, forcing an early retirement.

"Mark used to come on the away trips after he got diagnosed, he just wanted to be Mark - we had a good laugh everywhere we went," indicates Chandler. "He's still knocking about, abusing me on Facebook. He was the core of our second and third year.".

Whitley Bay lift the trophy in 2010, joined by former team-mate Mark Taylor (left).

Success ensured the lives of Chandler and his team were never quite the same again. Reporters turned up to Sage to speak with the manager and his players; even Chandler's mum was interviewed by BBC Radio Newcastle legend Paul Dixon.

Chandler - and his wife - even got up close and personal with managerial icons.

"I was invited to the annual sports awards in Manchester. There were people there like Sven Goran Eriksson and Sir Alex Ferguson [and] numerous others," he says.

"I had my wife with me and Sven came over gave her a peck on the cheek - she wasn't aware of who it was until I told her later that evening.".

Robinson admitted that going back to work at an IT firm after Wembley glory was a "massive comedown".

"One year I got a standing ovation when I walked into the office, but after that it was just back to normal," he notes.

It has been revealed that "People wind you up about it - 'are you talking about Wembley again? Give it a rest Robbo!".

According to recent reports, like all good things, Whitley Bay's golden era came to an end. Chandler departed in 2014 after a dip in form; the club have not won a major honour since the 2011 FA Vase and remain in the ninth tier.

But the memories in the football-mad north-east remain.

"Me and my wife went out on a Sunday at a pub in Durham just a few weeks back, and this guy came up out the blue and asked, 'Are you Ian Chandler?'" he laughs.

Sources indicate that "Then he started talking about that team; in the north-east, everyone follows football. It was so lovely.".

Latest Update: West Ham are in danger of becoming the next Leicester

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1140 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fourfourtwo

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Relegation can be the best thing that can happen to a club.
  • It offers the chance to reset, for fans to enjoy going to games again and for the team to come back stronger, with a clearer proposal and greater purpose.
  • Sources indicate that sometimes, though, relegation is just the start.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Relegation can be the best thing that can happen to a club.

It offers the chance to reset, for fans to enjoy going to games again and for the team to come back stronger, with a clearer proposal and greater purpose.

Sources indicate that sometimes, though, relegation is just the start. If it is not taken seriously, relegation might not be rock-bottom, but a trapdoor that sends a club spiralling to new lows.

Leicester City know all about that trapdoor. The Foxes were Premier League champions in 2016, FA Cup winners in 2021 and Conference League semi-finalists in 2021/22, but are now in League One after a series of relegations.

They were an established top-flight club, with a very competitive budget and had recently lifted major silverware, but years of poor decisions by an unpopular hierarchy saw them fall into the second tier and beyond.

West Ham United were an established top-flight club, with a very competitive budget and had recently lifted major silverware - the Conference League in 2023 - but dropped out of the Premier League last season after years of poor decisions by an unpopular hierarchy.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

The Hammers had been in the division since 2012 and finished as high as sixth in 2020/21, ending the campaign a place and a point behind Leicester. In 2024/25, the season before they went down, they generated the 20th-highest revenue in world football, according to the Deloitte Money League. Leicester were 17th in the Money League in 2021/22, the campaign before the first of their two recent relegations from the Premier League.

In a recent development, both clubs boast facilities that are out of place in their division. West Ham’s 62,500-seater London Stadium has almost double the capacity of the next biggest Championship ground, while Leicester’s training complex is one of the best in the country, let alone League One.

The parallels do not end there. Like Leicester 12 months ago, West Ham were one of the pre-season Championship promotion favourites and started the campaign well, but those results papered over the cracks.

Since climbing to second with a 1-0 victory at then-leaders Swansea City on October 17, the Hammers have gone six games without a win and sacked manager Nuno Espirito Santo, replacing him with Scott Parker. They are 13th ahead of today’s visit of second-place Stoke City, with 24 points from 17 matches.

It is eerily similar to Leicester’s start to last season. Looking to make an immediate return to the Premier League, the Foxes were third on October 17. But like West Ham, results started to slide. Like West Ham, they had 24 points after 17 games.

Of course, Leicester’s season ended with relegation, and the Hammers are by no means destined for the drop. Right now, though, the parallels are impossible to ignore.

Sources indicate that in terms of individual quality, both clubs began their respective seasons with one of the most talented squads in the league. Leicester had the likes of Abdul Fatawu, Jordan James and Stephy Mavididi, while West Ham can call on Jarrod Bowen, Konstantinos Mavropanos and Manor Solomon, among others.

However, both squads bore the hallmarks of years of poor recruitment. Leicester’s group included several substantial-money signings that had failed to deliver, including Patson Daka, Oliver Skipp and Jannik Vestergaard, and they did not pay a single transfer fee in the summer 2025 window to try to balance the books.

Meanwhile, West Ham have a top-heavy squad filled with attacking quality but light on defensive cover. The Hammers spent almost £40million this summer - including paying an EFL-record £22m for midfielder Arne Engels from Celtic - yet failed to address some glaring gaps in the squad.

It has been revealed that with all those attackers, West Ham need a manager who wants to dominate games. But Nuno prefers to let the opponents have the ball and attack rapidly in transition, which was ill-suited to his squad. The Hammers have now appointed Parker, a Championship promotion specialist having previously taken Fulham, Bournemouth and Burnley up.

In a recent development, once again, it is strikingly similar to Leicester, who sacked Marti Cifuentes in January and turned to Gary Rowett, a Championship survival specialist. However, his pragmatic style did not get the best out of his players and the Foxes continued to slide.

This runs deeper than the managers, though. Any head coach at Leicester would have struggled to reinvigorate a group of players who had either lost belief or did not want to be at the club anymore.

It has been revealed that that revealed in their reaction to going behind. After November 8 last year, Leicester did not win a single Championship game in which they conceded first. If heads drop when you suffer a setback, it points to a lack of confidence, fight or both, and form will suffer.

This season, West Ham are yet to win in the league after going 1-0 down, drawing five times and suffering five defeats. They have conceded first in every game of their six-match winless run. This is the biggest red flag of the Hammers’ season so far. Having quality players means nothing if they do not have the right mentality, as Leicester found out last term.

Industry observers note that it remains very unlikely that West Ham follow the Foxes into League One. But their recent transfer business does not suggest they will recruit smartly in January and if they miss out on promotion, you would expect some of their better players to leave next summer - sparking a transition period and potentially an extended spell outside of the top flight.

Sources indicate that even if Parker turns it around and wins promotion, is he the right man to lead them in the Premier League? The Hammers manager is yet to succeed in a top-flight job and if he is sacked in 12 months time, you would not back the club’s hierarchy to identify the right replacement based on their track record.

That was another feature of Leicester’s decline. The Foxes won promotion at the first attempt in 2023/24 but made poor managerial choices in Steve Cooper and then Ruud van Nistelrooy, and were relegated immediately.

Sources indicate that five years ago, West Ham fans would have dreamed of being the ‘next Leicester City’. Right now, it is the nightmare scenario.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Jamal Musiala will be sidelined “until further notice” after suffering a muscle injury to his right hamstring, in another setback for the 23-year-old.

Musiala has struggled with repeated injury issues over the last two years as well as a neurological condition which has received enormous scrutiny in recent weeks.

He suffered a muscle tear in April 2025 and began suffering from absence seizures, which cause a brief and sudden lapse in awareness, the same month, two months after signing a contract extension with Bayern Munich.

The condition was not made public knowledge until this summer, with Musiala experiencing two of these seizures during pre-season games. Absence seizures can be managed with daily medication, and other elite athletes, including England rugby player Tommy Freeman, have been able to continue professional sporting careers while experiencing the condition.

Over the same period Musiala has endured repeated injuries: he broke his fibula during the Club World Cup in 2025 and suffered a subsequent ankle injury, then had a metal plate removed from his foot after this summer’s World Cup.

Recent findings suggest that he has only recently returned from an absence induced by a hamstring tear, coming off the bench against Koln in the Bundesliga after two months out. He made an appearance as a second-half substitute in Bayern’s surprise 2-1 defeat to Lille in the Champions League this week, but has now suffered another setback.

Bayern Munich revealed on Friday: “FC Bayern’s medical department diagnosed Jamal Musiala with a muscle injury in his right thigh today. Musiala will be out until further notice. Get well soon, Jamal!”.

How Bayern have handled Musiala’s neurological condition has been heavily criticised after highly-publicised comments by several members of the club’s hierarchy.

Former board chairman Karl-Heinz Rummenigge cast doubt on the midfielder’s future, saying the “hefty sums of money” Musiala is paid are “not justifiable any longer”, and honorary president Uli Hoeness suggested his contract - which now runs until 2030 - should be reviewed if his illness and injury record prevents him returning to top form.

The comments sparked backlash, with players’ union Fifpro saying it was “deeply concerned” by the “pressure” placed on Musiala by such public remarks.

Stand-in captain Joshua Kimmich said after the Lille defeat: “What I don’t understand is the way this is being communicated in public. It must never happen that the burden is placed on a player. The club is obviously the top priority and bigger than a player, but it’s not bigger than a person. That’s an absolute no-go and it is not Bayern-like.”.

Bayern have a raft of top players out with injuries including star striker Harry Kane, who tore ligaments in his ankle during the Koln game, as well as Michael Olise, Manuel Neuer, Luis Diaz and Serge Gnabry.

They sit second in the Bundesliga and 15th in the Champions League group phase table.

#152331. The Unpromotables: Germany's league champions who can't go up

📅 02 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1791 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Co ↗ Open Full Page

The Unpromotables: Germany's league champions who can't go up

📅 02 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1791 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Djamal Ziane is a three-time league champion â but he does not always feel like it.
  • This summer, for the second year in a row and for the third time in seven seasons, the Lokomotive Leipzig captain hoisted the trophy into the air having led his team to the title in the Regional League Northeast, the fourth tier of German football.
  • But the memory is tinged with frustration because, just as in 2025 and 2020, Lokomotive's league title did not lead to promotion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Djamal Ziane is a three-time league champion â but he does not always feel like it.

This summer, for the second year in a row and for the third time in seven seasons, the Lokomotive Leipzig captain hoisted the trophy into the air having led his team to the title in the Regional League Northeast, the fourth tier of German football.

But the memory is tinged with frustration because, just as in 2025 and 2020, Lokomotive's league title did not lead to promotion.

According to recent reports, while the other regional champions in the German fourth division were promoted to the nationwide 3. Liga, "Lok" faced a play-off against a representative of the Regional League Bavaria, Wurzburger Kickers. Ziane scored, but an injury-ravaged Leipzig lost 3-1 on aggregate.

"Euer System ist krank," read a simple protest banner displayed by the 2,000 travelling supporters â "your system is sick".

"It's the worst thing â injury aside â that you can experience as a footballer," Ziane tells BBC Sport.

"Catastrophe doesn't cut it. It doesn't make any sense. If they really wanted to change it, they could do tomorrow.".

A banner reading 'Your system is sick' was displayed at this year's promotion play-off.

Germany's football pyramid has a bottleneck.

It has been revealed that beneath the Bundesliga, 2. Bundesliga and 3. Liga, the fourth tier is split into five regional divisions (North, West, Southwest, Northeast and Bavaria), each of which produces a league champion.

According to recent reports, so far, so good. But with only four teams being relegated from the 3. Liga each season, the sums don't add up.

An unsatisfactory solution is presently in place: the champions in the West and Southwest go up automatically while a third automatic promotion spot is rotated among the other three leagues in a three-year cycle. The fourth spot is allocated via a play-off between the winners of the remaining two leagues.

One champion always misses out and, increasingly, it's the champion from the Regional League Northeast, covering the territory of the former eastern German Democratic Republic (GDR).

In addition to Lok Leipzig's triple tragedy, former serial GDR Oberliga winners Dynamo Berlin fell short in 2022 and Energie Cottbus drew the short straw in 2023. This season, there is only one eastern German club in the 3. Liga: Hansa Rostock.

The struggles of the regions' football clubs are, to some degree, a result of continuing socio-economic disparities between east and west, which were also reflected in the success of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in recent state elections.

Industry observers note that even in 2026, not one of the 40 leading companies listed on Germany's DAX stock exchange is based in the former east (outside Berlin). Salaries remain lower, unemployment remains higher and the population is older and shrinking as young people move west.

The reason that automatic promotion spots are handed to the champions in the West and Southwest is simply because there are more men's football teams registered in those jurisdictions - because more people live there.

It is an argument that Ziane is tired of hearing.

"In that case, you might as well give us the automatic promotion spot because we attract bigger crowds," he indicates.

In a recent development, indeed, the average attendance in the Regional League Northeast last season (3,125) was around twice as high as that in the other leagues. Lok Leipzig themselves had the fourth highest (6,352). More than 11,000 attended the local derby against city rivals Chemie Leipzig.

"Unfortunately, you don't get any points for tradition, crowds and history," claims 39-year-old Lok chief executive Toni Wachsmuth, who does not have access to sponsors with the same financial firepower as his counterparts further west.

Sources indicate that "The [western] leagues do have better economic foundations but everyone agrees that the current system is nonsense. Everyone needs to compromise but some officials are clearly putting their own interests and positions above the general good of German football.".

It comes as little surprise, therefore, that the latest push for change has come from the east, with clubs launching a new campaign in March 2025 with the slogan: "Meister mussen aufsteigen!" â champions must go up!

Their proposal: a reduction from five leagues to four, with the precise geographical borders to be determined anew each season with the help of artificial intelligence, taking into account factors such as distance of travel to away games and attractive derbies.

They call it the compass model. Because it can go in all directions. In return, the Regional League Northeast is prepared to compromise by giving up its emotional attachment to the territory of the former East Germany.

Recent findings suggest that "I want to get away from this east-west debate," notes Tommy Haeder, the 35-year-old chief executive of Chemnitzer FC and figurehead of the reform campaign. "We've had a change of generation. Many older officials have retired and been replaced by younger people who don't have this nostalgia for the GDR.".

Haeder also emphasises the benefits that a fairer promotion system would bring for German football as a whole, arguing that eastern clubs would be better equipped to continue nurturing youth talent.

"It's not in the interest of talent development when young footballers from Chemnitz are torn away from their homes and families at the age of 10 to join academies in Hamburg, Dortmund or Stuttgart," he tells BBC Sport.

"The compass model is a model in which every region sacrifices a little bit to solve a much bigger problem. We're organised, we have a blueprint, we've made suggestions. Now it's up to the federations to act.".

The campaign has since gained the support of more than 80 clubs across Germany, from east to west and up and down the pyramid.

Union Berlin, who were playing in the fourth tier as recently as the 2000s, became the first Bundesliga club to officially back the initiative, with club president Dirk Zingler saying: "The current set-up contradicts our understanding of sporting competition.".

Borussia Dortmund president â and Bundesliga chairman â Hans-Joachim Watzke added his influential voice, stating: "Champions must go up and we think the compass model with four regional leagues is the best option.".

Support also has also come from Bournemouth head coach Marco Rose who, drawing on his past as both a player and coach at Lok Leipzig, stated: "I know what it's like for clubs trying to work within their means, or lack of means, at that level. Everything is on a knife edge.

"You have to give the clubs and their fans the belief that their efforts and sacrifices will be rewarded with promotion.".

Momentum was growing before a key vote at the end of June when, after months of discussions, clubs were finally set to vote on the compass model â but the ballot descended into farce when, at the last minute, the regional federations conducting the vote announced two key changes:.

Suddenly, the four new leagues would consist of only 18 teams rather than 20 (thus making the compass model less attractive because 10 more teams would miss out), and a stipulation was added that a majority be reached in each of the five regions for the model to pass.

An overall majority (50.9%) in favour of the compass model was still reached (including 60.9% in the West, 61.5% in the North and 76.3% in the Northeast) but the Southwest voted for an alternative option in which the northeastern league would be dissolved and its clubs reallocated, while the Southwest and West would simply remain the same.

"The move from a functioning system to a complex, insecure and economically riskier model without an obvious benefit doesn't make any sense to me," Robert Lempka, chief executive of Regional League Southwest side FSV Frankfurt told local public broadcaster Hessischer Rundfunk this summer. "I find it unsettling that an untransparent algorithm should decide a club's future.".

It has been revealed that the Bavarians, meanwhile, voted vaguely for "further talks", with Bavarian Football Federation (BFV) President Christoph Kern telling Munich's Abendzeitung newspaper in August: "We've gathered our clubs together on several occasions and none of the suggested models have majority support. I'm not prepared to simply give up the Regional League Bavaria like that.".

Sources indicate that for Haeder in Chemnitz, the vote was "an absolute catastrophe â completely amateurish". And he's not alone.

Recent findings suggest that this season, protests have erupted across German football. In the Regional League Northeast, almost every game has begun with a delay as players have simply refused to play for the first minute.

On the opening day, Lok Leipzig supporters, their team still stranded in the same division, threw hundreds of plastic trophies on to the pitch, symbolising the worthlessness of their club's back-to-back titles.

Down in Bavaria, Bayern Munich's ultras attended a reserve team game in the regional league and produced an intricate choreography criticising the Bavarian Football Federation (BFV) for what they perceive to be an unco-operative stance.

"You've taken us for fools long enough," read a banner beneath a display depicting BFV officials using a magnet to pull a compass needle towards them. The ultras then set off red pyrotechnics which turned the compass needle back in the direction of the fans.

In a recent development, and before the international break, fans of clubs across the Bundesliga used their platform to call for reform with co-ordinated banners reading: "Clubs and fans betrayed! Champions must go up! Compass model now!".

The compass, it would appear, may finally be pointing towards a resolution after the German Football Federation (DFB) unveiled the convening of an extraordinary general meeting on 18 December.

It has been revealed that "[The matter] must be resolved," mentioned President Bernd Neuendorf. "The compass model received the most votes and offers the best chance for a concentration of elite performance and therefore better development of talent.".

According to recent reports, any changes would only be implemented in the 2028-29 season â too late for Ziane who, now 34, has embarked on his 13th season with Lok Leipzig. Back-to-back champions, but still in the fourth division.

Recent findings suggest that "You can never completely get over it because, at our level, the 3. Liga is probably the pinnacle. Promotion with my hometown club would have been the most wonderful thing in the world for me," he indicates before heading out for training.

According to recent reports, "It's a shame that we have to force ourselves to remember what we've achieved. It's so hard to win this league and we did it twice in a row! You can't take that for granted.".
